title: A bill which would allow men accused of raping underage girls to be cleared if they marry the girl has been preliminarily backed by Turkish MPs.

In cities and towns across the country, people watched the results with a mix of curiosity and resolve, keen to see how the new administration would treat issues that matter most to them—the right to live without fear of discrimination, a future of thriving green energy, and the ability of Scottish universities to attract world-class researchers regardless of nationality. The First Minister’s spokesperson emphasised that Scotland’s relationship with the United States would be pursued with the same spirit that has underpinned the partnership for decades: mutual respect, shared interests, and a willingness to speak openly where positions diverge. In the days ahead, there was an expectation that Scottish leaders would be watchful for signals about how the new government planned to address issues that have long been areas of bipartisan interest in Scotland, including climate change commitments, free movement and the management of trade relationships with the European Union and other partners. It notes that sectors such as digital platforms, green investment, and flexible labour markets demand new measurement approaches and more frequent updates than have historically been the case. It also urges the creation of a structured framework for user engagement, including regular briefings with Treasury analysts, Bank of England economists and representatives from the OBR, as well as a formal mechanism for industry stakeholders to input into methodological decisions and release calendars. It argues that the ONS should publish more accessible explanations of methodology and uncertainty, and consider more frequent, shorter data releases where they add value. It notes that improved storytelling around statistics—clear descriptions of what the data show, what they cannot tell us, and the pace at which they are evolving—will help build public confidence. title: Speaking at the annual Munich Security Conference at the weekend, Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev claimed that Europe was "rapidly rolling into a period of a new cold war".
text_ai: "Russia," he said, "has been presented as well-nigh the biggest threat to Nato, or to Europe, America and other countries. "I am sometimes confused," he went on. "Is this 2016 or 1962?" German chancellor Angela Merkel, who has repeatedly urged dialogue with Moscow while defending Ukraine’s sovereignty, was reported to have told aides that Europe’s security architecture must be redesigned to be more resilient, even as it remains open to cooperation where possible. He warned that Moscow’s intent appeared to be to redraw borders and reassert influence by any means available—military, political and cyber. He said Russia’s actions in Ukraine, its support for proxies in other parts of Europe, and its aggressive behaviour in cyberspace posed a long-term threat to Western interests. “Russia may be pursuing a strategy of coercion, intimidation and subversion,” he said, underscoring that the United States would continue to work with allies to safeguard shared security goals. He argued that Western policies had effectively treated Russia as a permanent adversary, a stance he said had increased the likelihood of miscalculation. “If you treat Russia as the enemy, you will create enemies,” he said, adopting language that critics said echoed a long-standing Kremlin line that Western policymakers were seeking to isolate Moscow rather than engage it. Ukrainian officials used the conference to reiterate their demand for a credible end to Russia’s military campaign and for the full restoration of sovereign control over their eastern regions. With security budgets constrained, some defence ministers argued for smarter, not larger, forces — a focus on readiness, interoperability and the ability to deter pressure without triggering a costly arms race. The mood among some lawmakers and defence analysts was that a new era of strategic restraint was needed, but only if Russia itself demonstrated restraint and a genuine commitment to a rules-based order. Russia, for its part, has insisted that its actions are defensive and proportionate, a point repeatedly stressed by state media and by senior Russian officials. Moscow has argued that Western moves, including missile defence plans for Europe, threaten a strategic balance and compel Russia to respond. It also complains of what it portrays as double standards in the enforcement of sanctions and in the handling of the crisis in Ukraine, insisting that sanctions only entrench mistrust and make diplomacy more difficult. Energy security and economic pressures added another layer of complexity to the discussion. The Kremlin has long used energy as a tool of influence in Europe, a point analysts say remains true even as Moscow seeks to modernise its energy exports and diversify routes. Critics warn that the longer the crisis persists, the more Europe’s energy security is exposed to market volatility and political weather, even as European governments insist that diversification away from dependence on any single supplier must continue apace. In Kyiv, government officials noted that Moscow’s rhetoric and its continued support for separatist forces in eastern Ukraine continued to undermine prospects for a peaceful settlement. They cited ongoing casualties, displaced persons, and the difficult task of implementing reforms while the country confronts security threats on multiple fronts. They emphasised that Western solidarity, long a cornerstone of Ukraine’s security, remained essential in sustaining its resilience in the face of renewed pressure. Analysts at Munich warned that while the current crossfire of speeches risked obscuring some of the underlying strategic choices, Moscow’s ability to project influence in Europe would likely depend on a complex mix of diplomacy, economic pressure, and regional power moves. Some cautioned that any perception of a deliberate narrowing of channels for dialogue could backfire, hardening attitudes on both sides and eroding what little diplomacy was left in the channel between Moscow and the West. Officials from various capitals noted that while the international environment looked more brittle than it did a few years ago, there remained space for practical cooperation in limited areas where interests overlapped—counter-terrorism, stabilisation efforts in conflict zones, and humanitarian relief. Yet even there, participants acknowledged, the margins for error were slim, and misinterpretations could escalate quickly. On Sunday, organisers hoped to hear more concrete proposals to reinforce European security, to reassure nervous allies and to keep channels open with Moscow, even as national leaders prepared for a future in which dialogue and deterrence must somehow coexist. title: A seafood firm has called for Scottish-produced smoked salmon to be granted protected status.
text_ai: Moray-based Associated Seafoods said producers in other countries such as France and the US had "misappropriated" the Scottish tag for smoked salmon. It wants the product to be granted protected geographical indication (PGI) status. This would mean smoked salmon produced in other nations could not be packaged, sold or advertised as Scottish. The firm said the status would help protect the product from “bogus” labelling and would give consumers a clear, unequivocal signal about origin. A PGI designation would cover smoked salmon that is produced, cured or smoked in Scotland and that draws its distinctive character from the country’s supply chains and methods, according to the formal criteria. Industry observers say the move would be a long haul. Applicants must show that the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the product are essentially attributable to its geographic origin, and that at least one stage of production, processing or preparation occurs there. For smoked salmon, that is likely to mean salt curing and smoking takes place within Scotland, with Atlantic salmon sourced from the region. A spokesperson for Associated Seafoods said: “This is about protecting a precious Scottish heritage in seafood. Consumers deserve to know they are buying genuine Scottish smoked salmon, and producers deserve a level playing field against mislabelled imports.” The company did not detail how much a formal application would cost or how long the process would take. The Scottish Salmon Producers Organisation, which represents many Moray and Aberdeenshire farms, welcomed the proposal in principle but urged careful consideration of the practicalities. A senior figure said the sector already adheres to strict traceability and welfare standards, and that PGI status could bolster confidence in Scottish products both at home and abroad. “If the designation is well-designed, it could be a real benefit, provided it does not add unnecessary regulatory burdens,” they added. Opponents cautioned against a move that could complicate trade, particularly with international buyers who rely on flexible labels. A representative of a North American distributor said that while protecting regional brands is important, the cost and complexity of obtaining and maintaining PGI status could be challenging for smaller producers, potentially benefiting larger players with deeper pockets. The government response is likely to hinge on whether the designation fits within the UK’s post-Brexit framework for geographic indications. Officials would need to co-ordinate with devolved administrations and, if necessary, with European bodies to secure recognition. In practice, securing PGI protection would involve a formal application, consultation with stakeholders, and a demonstration of the link between place and product. If successful, a Scottish smoked salmon PGI could be introduced on labels with clear guidance about what counts as “Scottish” and which portions of the supply chain must occur within Scotland. Retailers said any such designation would need to be accompanied by broad consumer education so shoppers understand the criteria and can distinguish genuine Scottish salmon from other brands. Associated Seafoods said it would publish further details of its proposed route to PGI status in the coming weeks and would seek meetings with policymakers, processors and retailers to map out the path forward.

title: The keyboard and mouse have long been the main bridge between humans and their computers.
text_ai: More recently we've seen the rise of the touchscreen. But other attempts at re-imagining controls have proved vexing. "It's one of the hardest problems in modern computer science," Michael Buckwald, chief executive and co-founder of Leap Motion, told the BBC. The idea of a hand itself becoming a controller has repeatedly raised overhyped expectations and, at times, stubborn practical obstacles. In practice, translating a fluid, unconstrained motion into precise on-screen actions has proven tremendously tricky to perfect at scale. Leaps forward in prototyping have often led to bottlenecks in manufacturing, software compatibility, and, crucially, user experience. Leap Motion’s early hardware work epitomised the ambition: a tiny sensor that sat on a desk or laptop, watching your hands drift and gesture in three dimensions. For a while, developers imagined a future where you could float something in the air and manipulate it with a simple flick, pinch, or sweep. But even with clever software and algorithms, capturing natural movement with reliability across different lighting conditions and room layouts proved difficult. So did teaching millions of users to adopt a new set of gestures in order to accomplish basic tasks that keyboards and mice have long handled with ease. The market’s experiments in gesture control have sometimes felt like a series of near-misses. The launch and subsequent retreat of Microsoft's Kinect a decade ago became a cautionary tale: a sensor that could map full-body motion promised powerful new ways to interact, but required space, dedicated software support, and a leap of faith from developers. For many consumers, the novelty wore off long before the technology became indispensable. The result, industry watchers say, is a pattern of enthusiasm followed by pragmatism: aims high, deploy selectively, adjust, and move on. In recent years, however, a new generation of gesture-related tech has kept the idea alive by pairing tracking with other sensory feedback and by targeting specific tasks. Ultraleap, the company formed from the merging of hand-tracking and mid-air haptics technologies, has pushed a more contained model: users can see and track their hands and receive non-contact “feels-like” feedback through sonic and air-based actuators. The intent is not to replace keyboards and mice but to complement them in environments where touch is inconvenient or impractical—such as public kiosks, automotive displays, or operating rooms where physical contact is restricted. Analysts say the appeal now rests on practical use cases rather than broad, universal control. “The killer application is not waving at your screen, but enabling hands-free work in contexts where touching a device is impractical or unhygienic,” says Li Wei, a senior analyst at TechHorizons. “That means enterprise, healthcare, and industrial settings, where there’s real value in reducing contact with surfaces.” Eye-tracking has emerged as another route toward more natural interfaces. Integrated into some high-end laptops and external monitors, it promises cursor control and user authentication based on where you look. When combined with artificial intelligence, eye-tracking can anticipate what you want to do next, potentially speeding up routine tasks. Yet privacy concerns linger: cameras watching your gaze patterns can reveal sensitive information about attention, intent, and even health. Companies emphasise on-device processing and strict data controls, but observers say the industry must maintain transparency about what data is gathered and how it is used. Voice control has matured to the point where many people already rely on it daily for quick tasks—from dictating messages to searching the web. But speech interfaces still face limits. In noisy environments, or when multiple people speak in the same space, accuracy can drop. And for some tasks, speaking aloud feels intrusive or inefficient in a shared workplace. Still, advocates point to improvements in on-device AI that reduce latency and protect privacy, along with new “wake-word” and gesture-triggered combinations that aim to switch on hands-free modes only when needed. The frontier that draws much attention—and some cautionary headlines—is the realm of brain-computer interfaces. Early-stage research explores whether tiny implants or non-invasive sensors could translate neural activity into commands. Experts stress that it remains far from mainstream use and is surrounded by ethical, safety, and regulatory questions. “We’re still in the realm of exploratory science,” says Professor Anika Rahman, who studies neurotechnology at Imperial College London. “Even where progress is evident, it’s a long road from laboratory demo to everyday device.” For users with mobility or dexterity challenges, even incremental progress can feel significant. Accessibility advocates say gesture-based input, voice, and gaze controls together could offer alternatives when traditional input devices are impractical. But to realise these benefits widely, developers must ensure that such interfaces add value rather than complicate tasks. “The risk is tech for tech’s sake,” says Maria Santos, an accessibility consultant. “Interface design must be driven by real needs and proven improvements in comfort and efficiency.” In the consumer market, the consensus among many hardware makers is that the keyboard and mouse, though older, still deliver unsurpassed speed and precision for a broad range of tasks. The question is whether new modes of input will carve out meaningful, scalable niches that justify investment. Some devices now embed gesture sensing not as the primary control, but as a contextual helper—correction tools for creative software, or touchless shortcuts that reduce hand travel between keyboard and screen. Industry observers emphasise that progress will likely come in layered, hybrid systems rather than a single paradigm supplanting the traditional desktop. A screen may be controlled by a combination of voice, eye movement, and a subtle hand gesture, with the keyboard used for detail work or long-form typing. In such a future, the objective isn’t purely to replace a familiar tool but to augment it—reducing friction, increasing accessibility, and enabling new workflows in places where conventional controls would be awkward or cumbersome. Whether these breakthroughs will translate into a durable mainstream shift remains unclear. The coming years will test developers’ ability to deliver frictionless experiences, the resilience of software ecosystems to support novel inputs, and the willingness of users to adopt and adapt. For now, the keyboard and mouse endure in most professional settings, their dominance a reminder that in technology as in life, the simplest solution often endures longest. But the push to remove or reduce dependence on physical controls continues, driven by a vision of computing that responds as intuitively as a thought and as naturally as a gesture—without requiring a hand to be glued to a device.

title: A terminally-ill pensioner died minutes after being moved twice between hospital beds against her family's wishes, her sons have said.

title: A record number of people have complained after a French TV presenter posted a spoof ad on a gay dating website and made fun of people who responded live on air.

ARCOM said it had opened a formal inquiry under the country’s rules governing dignity, non‑discrimination and hate speech, and that it would assess whether the sequence breached the codes applicable to on‑air content. LGBT+ organisations said the stunt exploited gay dating sites to ridicule people who answered live, arguing it normalised harassment and reinforced stereotypes. “This was not humour,” said Sophie Rabier of a Paris-based campaign group. “It was an act of humiliation that left participants feeling degraded and frightened.” Campaigners called for accountability and an immediate review of the programme’s placement in the schedule. C8, the channel broadcasting the show, issued a separate statement saying it would conduct its own internal review of the segment’s production and editing. It emphasised that while the programme is intended to entertain, it does not condone harassment or discrimination and that it would consider any recommended changes to editorial practices. Human rights groups noted that the incident comes amid ongoing debates in France about freedom of expression, online platforms, and safeguarding communities from mockery and abuse. Critics argued that high‑profile presenters have a responsibility to avoid stoking hostility toward already marginalised groups, while supporters argued that audiences should expect provocative material as part of late‑night entertainment. The investigation could determine whether any sanctions are warranted, including fines or corrective measures, though regulators emphasised that any outcome would strictly follow established procedures. No timetable has yet been set for a decision.

title: A "bed-bound" woman died in a house fire in Ceredigion, an inquest has heard.

I kept shouting her name, but I couldn’t get to her.” Fire investigators who attended the scene said the blaze was contained largely to the interior living area and that rapid smoke development would have made rapid evacuation extremely difficult for anyone who was bed-bound. title: The morning after the EU referendum - before she had even been to bed - Scotland's First Minister Nicola Sturgeon said she thought another independence referendum was "highly likely".
text_ai: Since then she has upgraded that prediction several times from "more likely" to "almost necessary". The messaging has been pitched as a practical response to new circumstances rather than a bid to keep a political vow alive for its own sake. But the political weather in Edinburgh and Westminster has not made the path easy. Westminster ministers have warned that a second referendum would not be granted and could become a destabilising distraction from pressing domestic priorities. The UK government argues that the 2014 independence referendum settled the question for a generation, and that the focus should be on delivering Brexit and building a shared future for the United Kingdom as a whole. The Scottish Conservatives have pressed the government to resist any attempt to re-run the constitutional question while the country remains committed to the union. Labour, while offering sympathy to those who want a vote, has argued that a referendum should be timed to reflect a clear majority in favour and a settled economic case, which critics say has not yet emerged. The SNP’s strategy has therefore hinged on building a narrative that constitutional choices matter more when the UK’s departure from the EU is moving ahead in ways that could redefine Scotland’s economic and political landscape. It is a theme that has found resonance among sections of the public unsettled by the complex and often painful negotiations in Brussels and London, even as other voters remain cautious about re-entering a political contest that could bring more uncertainty rather than resolution. Analysts say the SNP has sought to keep the pressure on Westminster by framing the question as one of democratic legitimacy and national self-government, while positioning Scotland in the European orbit as a potential future member state should independence prevail. This stance has required careful handling of the economic debate, including the currency question and the implications for public spending, borrowing, and growth. Economic and constitutional questions sit at the heart of the debate. The Bank of England and several independent forecasters have warned that a rapid and disruptive transition could pose risks to Scotland’s economy, while proponents of independence argue that self-government would allow Scotland to pursue bolder policies tailored to its own needs. The urgency of these debates has grown as businesses, unions, and civic groups have weighed the potential paths ahead—whether to stay in the UK while rethinking certain arrangements or to pursue a clean break and rebuild around new institutions. The Scottish Parliament’s constitutional questions unit has begun mapping out scenarios in which a referendum could be held under different legal routes and political conditions. The most discussed route remains a Section 30 order—the formal legal agreement from Westminster that would allow Holyrood to schedule a binding poll. With the British government’s position that a referendum should not be offered, the likelihood of such an agreement has been uncertain, though not categorically ruled out. The potential for a vote, in turn, would hinge on shifts in public opinion, the scale of any economic disruption caused by Brexit, and whether a government at Westminster decides to alter its stance in response to Scotland’s devolved sentiment. In Scotland’s urban and rural communities alike, the referendum question has become part of the annual political fabric. Local councils have held debates, civic forums have highlighted concerns about public services, and business leaders have warned of the challenges and opportunities that could arise from different constitutional futures. The SNP argues that independence would give Scotland the levers to chart a path that aligns with its values, its economy, and its place in Europe. Unionist parties stress stability and the need to focus on practical policy issues that affect people’s daily lives. As party conference season approaches, Sturgeon is expected to outline further the case for a vote—what conditions would trigger it, what the timetable might look like, and what a post-independence Scotland would aim to achieve on the world stage. For opponents, the question remains whether the timing will ever feel right enough to cross the threshold of public consent, and whether the path to a referendum could become as fraught as the one that preceded it. The coming months will test whether the independence question endures as a live political project or retreats to the margins of policy debate. For now, the central tension remains clear: how Scotland can secure its future in a manner that commands broad consent, delivers economic security, and meets the expectations of a populace that has shown, at times, a wary and divided opinion on whether independence is the answer.

title: HSBC is the first big UK bank to explain in detail how it intends to get round the new European Union prohibition on big bonuses and continue to pay its top people many millions of pounds each.
text_ai: There are two ways of seeing its plans: either as sticking two fingers up to Brussels, in a way that maybe is not appropriate for such a big and important institution; or as demonstrating the madness of the EU's attempt to curb local behaviour, in this case the pay of bankers, in businesses which have to compete in a global market. The bank acknowledges that the aim of the cap is to curb excess while preserving stability in the global financial system. But, in its briefing, HSBC argues that properly designed remuneration can still reward risk- and performance-driven decision-making without encouraging reckless short-termism. Under the plan, a larger portion of what would historically have been cash bonuses would be redirected into long-term, equity-based awards that vest over several years. The idea, HSBC says, is to tie a meaningful slice of reward to sustained performance and to the creation of shareholder value, rather than to a single year’s results. The awards would be subject to sophisticated deferral provisions, with clawback mechanisms if risk controls breach thresholds or if later performance deteriorates. A further element involves adjustments to the way some pay is delivered within the fixed pay envelope. HSBC argues that by offering higher base salaries for top roles, while deploying more limited, but longer-dated, variable pay, it can meet the letter of the EU cap while still maintaining competitive compensation packages. In practice, that could translate into higher fixed pay for a handful of executives, complemented by multi-year equity awards and contingent retention bonuses that vest only if risk and performance metrics are met. The plan also emphasises governance safeguards. Any performance-related awards would be anchored to clear milestones for shareholder value, risk-adjusted return, and risk management, with independent oversight to prevent perverse incentives. The briefing reiterates that awards would carry malus provisions and would be clawed back in the event of material misconduct or if risk controls fail in subsequent years. Regulators’ reaction is likely to hinge on the details. Brussels officials have signalled that the purpose of the cap is to curb short-term, cash-heavy pay while preserving incentives for long-term value creation. A Brussels spokesperson said that the bloc would scrutinise any structure claimed to comply with the rules “on the basis of its functional design, its alignment with risk, and its impact on financial stability.” The official added that the equal priority would be given to transparency and accountability to avoid any perception of gaming the framework. Industry analysts say the plan, if implemented with robust governance and transparent reporting, could represent a standard-bearer for how banks navigate the cap while keeping senior talent engaged. “This is a textbook example of pay engineering,” one senior analyst said. “The critical test will be whether the equity-based elements retain genuine accountability for risk and whether the deferral terms are credible enough to deter excessive risk-taking.” HSBC insists the policy is not about chasing headlines or gaming a regulatory boundary. It says its remuneration framework is designed to attract, retain, and motivate senior leaders who can steward the bank through volatile markets while maintaining prudent risk controls and strong capital discipline. For investors, the plan warrants close scrutiny in the coming months. If regulators sign off, HSBC could set a template for how major banks balance global competitiveness with EU rules. If not, the bank will face renewed pressure to recalibrate its approach, with implications for executive compensation across the sector. The next phase will unfold as Brussels weighs the specifics and looks for assurances that pay truly serves long-term stability rather than short-lived gains.

title: A review into Northern Ireland's health service has said there are too many hospitals for the 1.8 million population.
text_ai: The review was led by the former chief medical officer of England, Sir Liam Donaldson. The review makes a total of 10 recommendations. It contends that the region’s current spread of hospitals leads to duplication, uneven access to specialist care and higher costs, and that a more geographically rational model would improve outcomes for patients with time‑critical conditions such as stroke, heart attack and major trauma. It stops short of prescribing an exact number of sites, but it makes clear that the current configuration is unlikely to be viable in the long term without substantial change. A second strand focuses on the patient journey. It says primary care must be strengthened so people can access timely advice and treatment without resorting to emergency or urgent care routes where inappropriate. Third, the authors stress the need for a major upgrade in elective and planned care. They propose a move towards a greater share of day‑case surgery, more efficient use of operating theatres, and a single, regionally coordinated waiting list to reduce postcode‑lottery type delays. The aim, the report states, is to shorten waits for typical elective procedures while maintaining high safety and quality standards. Fourth, the urgent and emergency care system would be reorganised around integrated urgent care hubs. These centres would combine a GP‑driven front door with rapid access to diagnostics, and tightly integrated ambulance services to ensure patients are directed to the right service first time. Seventh, digital and data systems would be overhauled to enable a single, interoperable patient record across the health service and to support real‑time performance monitoring. The commissioners would be given stronger access to analytics to direct investments where they would have the greatest impact on outcomes and throughput. Eighth, public health and prevention would be treated as central to the reforms. The report argues for a more proactive focus on lifestyle, vaccination, early intervention and mental health, arguing that improved population health would reduce demand on hospital services over time. Ninth, integration with social care and broader community services would be intensified. title: Saturn's ice-crusted moon Enceladus may now be the single best place to go to look for life beyond Earth.
text_ai: The assessment comes on the heels of new observations at the 500km-wide world made by the Cassini probe. It has flown through and sampled the waters from a subsurface ocean that is being jetted into space. Cassiniâ€™s chemistry analysis strongly suggests the Enceladean seafloor has hot fluid vents - places that on Earth are known to teem with life. The team behind the measurements says the implications extend far beyond Enceladus’ ice-shell. If there is a long-lived, chemically rich ocean beneath the crust, and if hydrothermal activity is delivering energy and nutrients to the seafloor, then the moon could host a microbial ecosystem, perhaps akin to those thriving in Earth’s deep-sea vents. The plume data, gathered over multiple passes through the geyser-like jets, show a cocktail of water vapour, ice grains, salts and organic compounds. The salts, largely composed of carbonates and chlorides, point to a salty ocean in contact with a rocky interior. The presence of silica-rich grains hints at high-temperature interactions at or near the ocean floor, where heated water could be leaching minerals from the rock. And the detection of hydrogen in the plume—a byproduct expected when expanding seawater contacts hot, rocky material—has become the talking point for astrobiologists, because hydrogen can serve as a readily available chemical energy source for microbial life. “Enceladus is a laboratory in space for studying how life-sustaining chemistry could work,” said Dr Helena Ortiz, a planetary scientist at the Institute for Space Studies. “The combination of liquid water, a rocky interior, and a steady supply of chemical energy through hydrothermal-like processes makes this world uniquely compelling.” The findings, while not proof of life, strengthen a growing view that some of the most promising places to search for life in the Solar System are the ocean worlds hidden beneath thick ice. Enceladus, a moon barely a thousand kilometres across, has become a poster child for that idea, outshining other candidates in the Saturnian system because a single fly-through can sample material from its hidden ocean. The Cassini team stresses that the data are consistent with a sustained, heat-driven exchange between a subsurface ocean and the moon’s rocky core. On Earth, hydrothermal vents support ecosystems that require no sunlight, relying instead on chemical energy. While there is no direct evidence of organisms on Enceladus, the mere presence of energy-rich chemistry in the plume is “a big step toward understanding the habitability of this world,” in the words of one scientist involved in the mission. Scientists acknowledge the leap from chemistry to biology is large. The same plume that offers tantalising clues also complicates the search for signs of life. Some molecules detected could be produced abiotically, by non-biological geological processes. Distinguishing between life-generated signatures and inorganic chemistry will demand new instruments and carefully designed missions in the years ahead. To that end, missions proposed to follow up Cassini’s discoveries are already under discussion in scientific circles and space agencies. One possibility is a dedicated probe capable of drilling through the ice shell or, alternatively, repeatedly sampling the plumes as they spew into space, analysing the composition of ice grains and vapour with greater sensitivity. A mission that could return samples to Earth—or at least bring back pristine plume material—would allow analyses far beyond what is possible with remote sensing. Professor Nisha Kapoor, who chairs an astrobiology programme in London, emphasised the need for caution. “A positive signal in chemistry can inspire a narrative, but life detection requires a suite of confirmatory tests,” she said. “If future missions can measure stable, long-lived chemical disequilibria, or—ideally—biosignatures that are difficult to reproduce abiotically, then the case for life becomes much stronger.” The Enceladus discovery also reframes the broader hunt for life beyond Earth. Europa, another icy moon with a subsurface ocean beneath its own frozen crust, has long been considered the front-runner for a dedicated mission. The current Cassini results, however, have shifted some of the attention toward a more nuanced view: multiple ocean worlds may exist in the outer Solar System, each offering distinct but complementary pathways to habitability. The coming decades could see a set of missions aimed at different targets, potentially building a more complete picture of how common life-supporting environments might be. For now, the Cassini scientists stress that the data are a clarion call for more exploration, not a closed case. The team will continue to pore over the mission’s archive and model the interior dynamics that could sustain hydrothermal activity for billions of years. They are also calling for a renewed emphasis on ice-shell dynamics—how cracks propagate, how heat is transported, and how material from the ocean is vented into space. If a future mission confirms that Enceladus harbours a living ocean, the discovery would carry profound implications not just for biology, but for how humanity understands its place in the cosmos. It would demonstrate that life can arise and persist in environments radically different from Earth, expanding the number of cosmic oases where life might take hold. In the coming months, scientists will publish more detailed analyses of the plume chemistry and its implications for ocean temperature, salinity and energy flux. The discussion will undoubtedly stretch beyond the technical, feeding into public imagination about life elsewhere and the next steps humanity might take in exploring the outer planets. What is clear is that Enceladus has moved from being a distant curiosity to a focal point for the search for life in the Solar System. As mission teams and space agencies weigh the options for future exploration, the icy moon’s jets—once seen as a spectacular byproduct of a cold world—have become a doorway to one of the most profound questions humans can ask: could life exist beyond Earth, in a world hidden beneath ice?

title: The idea that party leaders are decisively important in the winning or losing of general elections is implicit in much political journalism and it is a belief that some political leaders themselves - Tony Blair, in particular - have been eager to propagate.
text_ai: It is very rarely true. It is only in an extremely close-run race that the personality of the leader and the gulf between that leader's standing and the popularity of his or her principal opponent can make the difference between victory and defeat. It is not a simple equation, and it never has been. The public does not decide a general election on the quality of a single personality study or a short burst of televised performance alone. Yet the anxiety about whether a leader can "sell" an agenda to the country remains a constant feature of campaign coverage, a shorthand that tabloids and broadsheets alike reach for when the polling shows a cliff-edge between seats for one party and another. What the data most consistently shows is that the leader’s appeal moves the dial only when the challenger’s standing is markedly different from their opponent’s and when the electorate feels the choice before them is existentially about who should be entrusted with power. In those moments, a striking debate performance, a memorable slogan, or a perceived capacity to steer the ship in a crisis can tilt a handful of crucial constituencies. But in a British general election, those constituencies are often already reported through the lens of the party’s programme, the state of the economy, and long-standing attachments to a party’s brand. Labour’s 1997 breakthrough is frequently cited as the closest the modern political era gets to a cautionary tale about the limits of personality while still conceding a decisive role for leadership. Tony Blair entered the campaign with a revitalised image of modernisation and reform, but the scale of his triumph owed much to the public mood for change and to a party that had remade itself in a way that many voters perceived as credible on the economy, on public services, and on Britain’s place in the world. The leader’s personal appeal amplified that mood, yet it did not solely create it. The party’s careful articulation of policy, the discipline of its campaign, and the sense that Labour could be trusted to govern were the bigger engines of the result, with Blair’s charisma acting as a catalyst rather than the sole driver. Conversely, there are elections where the leader’s standing did not convert into victory, or where it mattered far less than the party’s overall trajectory. In campaigns where the public judged the governing party as having performed poorly on immediate concerns—be it the economy, the national deficit, or public services—the personal appeal of the opposition leader could be dampened by a broader scepticism about what change would actually look like in practice. In such cases the campaign becomes a referendum not on personality but on competence and continuity, and the party with the more persuasive long-term vision for governance tends to carry the day, irrespective of the leader’s stagecraft. The phenomenon is not simply a matter of “leader versus leader” in a televised duel. The terrain of British politics in which general elections unfold is shaped as much by the party’s overall offer as by the media narrative around its figurehead. Gravity is exerted by the economy, by the NHS, by education, by housing, by immigration and by the sense that a government can deliver stable, predictable policy over a full term. When a party has credible, coherent answers to those concerns, the leader’s profile can improve the mood around the party without changing the underlying arithmetic of votes. When a party lacks that coherence, a compelling personality may still win over a swathe of floating voters, but it seldom translates into a durable majority. Those dynamics are reinforced by the mechanics of the electoral system. The first-past-the-post model concentrates support in a relatively small number of marginal seats. In those seats, local candidates, campaign ground games, and the ability to translate national slogans into seat-specific promises matter as much as, if not more than, a leader’s national popularity. The arithmetic of swings across dozens of constituencies—where a few thousand votes here or there can decide a result—means that a party’s leadership can influence the outcome only insofar as it supports the broader momentum of the campaign. A party with a robust ground operation, disciplined messaging, and credible policy can ride a leader’s goodwill, but a leader who is seen as out of step with the party’s direction or with the electorate’s immediate concerns is unlikely to salvage a weak platform. This nuance helps explain why political analysts often push back against the idea that leaders carry every election on their shoulders. The reality, as many scientists and commentators have observed, is that leadership is one instrument among many in the campaign toolkit. The strength of a party’s manifesto, the state of the public finances, the perception of the economy’s direction, and the depth of public trust in institutions exert a much more durable influence on the ballot than any one politician’s personal charm. And in recent decades, as communications environments have intensified, leaders have found themselves both amplified by media attention and constrained by the inexorable gravity of policy outcomes. That is not to say leadership is irrelevant. There are moments when a leader’s reputation for steady stewardship or bold reform becomes the hinge on which a campaign turns. Debate performances, policy pivots, and the ability to project a clear, credible narrative can convert soft support into solid backing when the electorate is torn between competing visions. In these moments, the leader’s task is less to persuade the public of a new economic orthodoxy than to reassure them that their priorities will be pursued with competence, consistency, and accountability. The broader lesson, then, is that the leader acts as a conduit for much longer-standing forces—the party’s brand, policy credibility, and the public’s assessment of risk and governance. A strong leader can magnify those forces, hasten their pace, or direct them in a particular direction. A weak or unsettled leadership can diminish the impact of a seemingly strong platform, or fail to convey the seriousness of a compelling new programme. But neither personality nor campaign rhetoric is the sole determinant. For journalists and analysts, these insights carry an important responsibility. In the scramble of air-time and porch-door persuasion, there is a danger that the search for a single dramatic narrative—“will the leader win?”—overshadows the more consequential arithmetic of policy choices and national conditions. Voters deserve coverage that weighs the legitimacy of policy proposals alongside the charisma of the person presenting them. And leaders deserve scrutiny that goes beyond the soundbite to examine whether their promises are deliverable within the constraints of the economy, the constitution, and the country’s international obligations. In the run-up to any general election, the careful observer will track two parallel trajectories. One is the polling of leader approval, and the other is the polling of party allegiance and policy clarity. The former can wax and wane with a debate performance or a moment of crisis, but the latter tends to cluster around a broader assessment of who can govern effectively, who will protect public services, and who will steward the economy in the interests of everyday voters. The relative strength of those trajectories often explains why, even in the most intense campaigns, the winner is seldom decided by a single dramatic surge in leadership appeal. There is also a continuing shifting landscape to consider. The rise of issue-based voting, where voters align with a party because of a concrete policy stance on, for example, taxation, climate change, or immigration, can erode the traditional correlation between leader intensity and electoral fortune. In such cases, the electorate’s trust in a party’s ability to deliver practical solutions—rather than its capacity to present a compelling figure—becomes decisive. Conversely, in times of national crisis or great uncertainty, the electorate may crave reassurance from a steady, credible leader, even if their policy programme is not radical. The media environment itself shapes the outcome by how it frames the contest. Coverage that treats politics as a perpetual horse race can inflate the perceived importance of the leader at the expense of policy discussion. Conversely, reportage that foregrounds policy detail, costings, and implementation can help voters make judgments about the real-world consequences of a party’s promises, which, in turn, narrows the space in which personality can swing the result. As campaigns proceed, the public’s expectations will interact with those forces in unpredictable ways. The next general election, like those before it, will hinge less on whether a leader can conquer a moment with a single memorable soundbite and more on whether the party can present a credible, deliverable programme, and whether the country’s economic and social conditions favour the change that the opposition represents. The leader’s personal story will matter to some voters, and in particular to those making a choice in marginal seats where every vote counts. But for most, the vote will be cast on the balance of risks and benefits posed by the government-in-waiting and by the opposition’s ability to govern. In that sense, the enduring truth remains: the leader is a voice among many in a country that votes for a programme, a party, and a future. The air-time that surrounds that voice is valuable, but it is never the whole story. If general elections were won purely on personality, the history of British politics would look very different. Instead, the decisive factor is always a combination—the party’s offer, the state of the country, the mood of the electorate, and, yes, at times, the leader’s own capacity to translate those elements into a credible path to government. That is the challenge for any campaign and the benchmark against which voters, and observers, should measure results.

title: A study of the world's largest subway networks has revealed that they are remarkably mathematically similar.

title: The healthiest way to cook mushrooms is to microwave or grill them to preserve their goodness, researchers say.

title: The death of a close, elderly relative can often mean a sombre weekend or two going through old things, sorting through photographs, donating old clothes to charity.
text_ai: But in an age when so much of our lives are online, little thought has been given to how we handle a person's digital world when they are no longer with us. Legal and practical hurdles are confronted most often by those who are trying to administer an estate. The law in the United Kingdom has long treated digital data as part of a person’s estate in the sense that those who administer the estate must follow last wishes and applicable contracts, but it does not automatically hand over passwords or private information. Data protection rules complicate access to a dead person’s accounts, even when the executor is a close relative. Platforms will typically want proof of the executor’s authority, such as a grant of probate, a death certificate, and identity checks, before releasing any information or allowing changes to be made. Accompanying this, the everyday item of a password can be a barrier that policy cannot easily overcome. A survey of funeral directors and probate specialists found that families frequently discover that legacy settings and digital assets form the most challenging part of the process, often delaying the distribution of assets and the closure of accounts. Policy makers and industry bodies have urged clearer guidance for families. In recent years, think tanks and law reform bodies have pressed for a clearer framework that would recognise digital assets—photos stored in the cloud, emails, social media accounts, and even crypto wallets—as part of the estate, with a named person who can administer them in a legally recognised way. The aim is not to expose private information but to prevent needless loss of irreplaceable memories and to curb ongoing charges for subscriptions that the deceased no longer used. For those planning ahead, the message from experts is simple: start now. A will that includes digital assets, and a separate, up-to-date inventory of online accounts and access details, can save families weeks of struggle. The inventory should be stored securely, ideally with a trusted professional or in a password-managed system that the executor can access. It should specify which accounts to preserve for memory and which to close to avoid ongoing costs or risk of misuse; it should also indicate whether content such as photographs or messages should be shared with certain relatives or archived in perpetuity. One London solicitor who specialises in digital assets says the most common request from clients is for a concise, up-to-date plan. “People want to protect the family from a future scramble, and they want to ensure that their memories aren’t lost because someone can’t log in,” they said. “A basic checklist—possible accounts, what should be preserved, what should be deleted—can be the difference between a tidy closure and a prolonged, painful process.” Executors, too, face a steep learning curve. They must sift through the deceased’s digital footprint, notify platforms, and decide what should be archived for descendants or not. They may also need to contend with subscriptions that continue to charge, or with emails and messages that contain sensitive information that relatives may wish to protect from others. For many, the impact of not having a plan is about memory as much as money. The photos, the voice notes, the messages—these are the intimate record of a life. A well-handled digital legacy can be a balm, a way to share memories with children or grandchildren, and to keep a loved one’s online presence respectful and secure. A few families already report that, once the business of access is sorted, they find solace in the ability to retrieve a cherished album or a final message left by the deceased. The counsel to the living is plain: consider your digital life as you would your physical one. Name a digital executor, document your wishes, assemble a secure inventory, and speak with relatives about the kind of presence you want your online world to have after you are gone. In a world where every photo, every email, and every memory is just a click away, the peace of mind that comes from planning can be the best gift left behind.

Supporters of the withholding strategy say the fight is necessary to compel a broader reform of the healthcare system, arguing that any plan to maintain government funding should be tied to changes in Obamacare they view as essential. Describing the situation, Treasury officials warned there could be consequences if the holdout continued, including the risk of late payments on government contracts, delay in government-mathered services, and potential volatility in financial markets that have already grown twitchy in the face of political uncertainty. Analysts cautioned that a protracted shutdown could have a broader effect on the economy, by reducing consumer confidence and delaying construction, research and other federally funded projects. In the private sector and in civic groups, the mood ranged from anxious to defiant. Some business leaders urged lawmakers to resolve the funding dispute quickly, stressing that daily triage in the capital must not translate into a prolonged stall in the country’s business climate. Advocates for the federal workforce described the immediate consequences of furloughs: families facing delayed mortgages, loan payments and groceries, and the emotional strain of uncertainty over whether back pay would ever be owed. The political calculus remains delicate. Critics of the Obama administration say the White House has underestimated the leverage that a large, widely publicized shutdown can exert on public opinion and on the bargaining table. Supporters of the conservative stance insist the fight over Obamacare is not merely about a single law but about the future direction of government, and argue that a temporary saving could be worth the price of friction in the short term. Meanwhile, international observers and foreign governments have been watching closely. The interruption of routine federal functions, including some international programmes that rely on U.S. agencies, raised questions about how other countries should interpret Washington’s political theatre. In some capitals, diplomats urged restraint and called for a constructive dialogue that would restore normal operations as soon as possible, stressing that the disruption could complicate diplomatic work and international cooperation on issues ranging from climate change to security. As for the people on the ground, public services that are essential to daily life continued to function at varying levels. Social security and veterans’ benefits are generally considered essential and would continue in many cases. But even these core services could be affected if the stalemate persisted and the contours of funding and policy questions became more fluid. For many, the risk is not only the immediate loss of pay but the long-term worry that a political impasse could set back years of reforms and investment in sectors like science, infrastructure and education, where federal support plays a critical role. In Capitol Hill’s corridors, the argument over Obamacare’s fate continues to dominate conversations. The House insists any spending measure be linked to the defunding or delay of the healthcare reform, arguing that this is a moral and practical obligation to limit what they view as an overreach by the executive branch. The White House has singled out that demand as the central obstacle to reopening the government, and has pressed for a clean funding bill that would restore the status quo without reopening debate over the healthcare law’s architecture. For now, the immediate consequence is economic and administrative paralysis, a pause in the machinery that underpins a broad swath of public life. Vendors who operate on government contracts report uncertainty over payment schedules, while universities and scientific laboratories that rely on federal funding fear delays to ongoing projects and the potential loss of talent if researchers are left in limbo. The question for the country is how long the shutdown will last and what will end it. A number of lawmakers signalled that a return to business as usual depends on a willingness to compromise, but that willingness remains in question. Some have warned that shutting down the government is an intolerable option, a position that may gather more support as the cost of inaction becomes clearer to voters. Others argue that the situation is a necessary pressure point to extract changes to a system they believe needs broad reform. As the clock ticks, Americans watching the stalemate are left to navigate a fragile reality: a government that can plan for every contingency except the political one. The disruption serves as a reminder that, despite the country’s wealth and resilience, the machinery of government can falter when the political branches fail to bridge a fundamental divide over policy direction. Looking ahead, lawmakers on both sides prepared for a renewed round of discussions. A framework for a continuing resolution—short-term funding that would keep the government operating while a longer-term budget agreement is negotiated—was floated by some as a potential path out of the impasse. Yet any such plan would still require agreement on Obamacare, either in the form of a delay, modification, or the ceremonial removal from the political ledger of the contentious issue for a period of time, something that proponents on both sides have rejected at different moments. In a country where citizens expect the government to function, the shutdown stands as a stark test of democratic process. The hows and whys of the budget fight have dominated headlines for days, but the human consequences—families awaiting paychecks, students depending on federal aid, travellers facing delays—are now the defining reality for many Americans. Leaders at the city and state levels, as well as public workers’ unions and associations, have urged a rapid return to normality. They argued that while political disagreements may be inevitable in a large, diverse democracy, the practical need to deliver essential services cannot be postponed indefinitely without inflicting real damage. As political theatre and procedural knots continue to unfold in Washington, the country awaits a resolution that seems both urgent and elusive. At stake is not merely the mechanics of government, but the capacity of the United States to govern itself in the eyes of its citizens and the world beyond its borders. The coming days will reveal whether the cost of the fight will force a compromise, or whether the deadlock will be sustained until a broader agreement—one that could redefine the balance between reform and policy—emerges from the shambles of a government momentarily unable to pay its own bills.
prefix: The Republican-led House of Representatives insisted on delaying President Barack Obama's healthcare reform - dubbed Obamacare - as a condition for passing a bill. More than 800,000 federal employees face unpaid leave with no guarantee of back pay once the deadlock is over, as certain agencies and national parks also close.

title: After a week of disturbing headlines, is Islamic State winning?
text_ai: It depends where. In Syria, where Islamic State (IS) captured Palmyra and is said to have murdered large numbers of people in its usual bloodthirsty fashion, it looks as though the regime of Bashar al-Assad is getting into serious trouble. Its army is no longer so effective at fighting his battles. Outside Syria, the picture is anything but uniform. In the gap between flashpoint frontlines and fragile provincial towns, Islamic State’s reach has become, for many observers, a test of the region’s long-term political and military stamina rather than a straightforward indicator of a collapsing order. In Palmyra, the militants’ assault has exposed a widening fault line between the regime’s military capabilities and its political will to prosecute a long war on multiple axes. The army, once the backbone of Assad’s grip on the country, has struggled to hold and hold together a network of frontlines that stretch from the Mediterranean to the gates of Damascus. For now, loyalist forces have regrouped around major cities, but there is little sign of a rapid, decisive reversal of IS gains in the more remote desert regions and in outlying towns along the highway networks that the militants have exploited for supply and reinforcements. Analysts say the group’s ability to seize and hold territory is no longer enough on its own to claim that it has won a broader war. “IS’s strength lies in its capacity to move quickly, to create a state-like aura in places it controls, and to intimidate populations enough to force people to flee or to collaborate,” said a Middle East specialist in London. “But holding a city is a different matter. Once you take a place, you have to govern it, you have to supply it, you have to incorporate or suppress its people. That is a different, longer test.” In Iraq, the mood is similarly mixed. The militants retain an entrenched presence in parts of Anbar, and their momentum in the north and west has unsettled rather than destroyed the broader coalition effort to push back across the Euphrates valley. American-led airpower, combined with Iraqi security forces and Kurdish peshmerga units, has delivered a steady stream of setbacks for the group in some towns, while other areas have fallen in days and then remained under IS control for weeks. The risk, Western officials say, is a repetition of a pattern in which fighters retreat from one town only to reappear elsewhere, replenished by a pipeline of foreign recruits and local sympathisers who see the “caliphate” as an alternative to the chaos they are living in. On the ground, the humanitarian situation remains crushing. Aid agencies say thousands have fled Palmyra and surrounding districts, many of them now dispersed in camps and makeshift settlements across the desert. For communities that had endured years of civil conflict and displacement, the return of IS control to any town carries with it the drama of reprisals, forced conversions or collaborations, and the ever-present threat that a single, brutal night could erase years of fragile normality. There is, too, a significant counterbalance to IS’s territorial ambitions that often goes under the radar: the Kurdish-led forces in the north and the multinational efforts to keep the group out of major urban centers. In several fronts, Kurdish units, backed by a broader coalition, have reclaimed towns previously under IS control and pushed the militants away from critical corridors. In some areas, residents report a sense of temporary relief as checkpoints are re-established and the threat of mass religious persecution is reduced, at least for the moment. Still, the battle lines are blurred by the politics of the allies’ own goals. For Moscow, the Syrian front is inseparable from a larger geostrategic contest with the West and regional rivals. For Washington, the priority has been to prevent IS from returning to its 2014–15 apex of territorial control while creating enough space for local partners to stabilise what remains of the territory. And for regional powers, the calculus includes protecting allies, shoring up fractured governance, and avoiding a new wave of mass displacement that would ripple across borders. The group’s leadership is said to be adapting its tactics. Rather than simply clinging to a shrinking core of towns, IS is believed to be consolidating a network of fortified outposts and supply hubs, seeking to keep the flow of men and weapons open and to project an image of resilience through propaganda and spectacular violence. In the absence of a single, decisive battlefield victory, its success is being measured in the staying power of its influence, the endurance of its narrative, and the ability of its fighters to exploit the missteps of rival forces. Civilians in contested zones describe a world where fear is a constant companion. One Palmyra resident who fled after a recent siege spoke of the “silence that follows the gunfire” and the sudden, brutal shifts in control that force people to abandon the routines of daily life. Aid workers say the most urgent immediate needs are for shelter, food, and protection against further violence, but longer-term concerns loom large: the prospects for schooling, healthcare, and reliable governance are dim in places where IS remains a credible threat and where the state’s writ does not run. In Washington and in capitals across Europe and the Middle East, officials stress that a victory is not defined solely by the territory IS can or cannot hold. The real test, they say, is the extent to which communities can be rebuilt, how quickly people can return to normal life, and whether the group can be deprived of its most potent weapon—a sense of permanence and inevitability that can draw in recruits from abroad. So, while Palmyra’s fate has become a potent symbol of IS’s renewed reach, experts caution against drawing hasty conclusions about a wider strategic success. The battlefield is fragmented, the alliances are febrile, and the human cost continues to mount. For now, the question remains: is Islamic State winning? The answer, as ever in this conflict, depends on where you measure, and who you ask. What is indisputable is that the war will go on, and the consequences will be felt well beyond the frontlines for years to come.

title: A major US conservative forum has dropped Donald Trump as a speaker, saying it was unacceptable for him to suggest that a journalist was tough on him because she was menstruating.
text_ai: Mr Trump said Megyn Kelly of Fox News "had blood coming out of her eyes, blood coming out of her wherever". Ms Kelly had challenged him on remarks he made about women during a TV debate. Amid the controversy it emerged that Mr Trump's top political adviser had left his campaign. The Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) announced that Mr Trump would not take part in this year’s programme, saying his remarks about Megyn Kelly were “unacceptable” and inconsistent with the forum’s standards. In a statement the organisers said they would not provide a platform for attacks that demean or belittle journalists, particularly on the basis of gender or physiology. The decision, they added, was taken after careful consideration of the tone and content of the comments in question and their potential to overshadow the event’s aims of debating policy and safeguarding civil discourse. The move marks a sharp rebuke from one of the most influential gatherings on the American right, coming at a time when Mr Trump’s campaign has been increasingly defined by personal controversy as much as by policy proposals. The forum’s board emphasised that it remained open to vigorous debate and to candidates who could articulate a vision for the country, but that inflammatory personal attacks would not be tolerated. In Washington, the campaign responded with a defiant note, saying the decision reflected a broader pattern of attempts to silence Mr Trump and to define him by one set of remarks taken out of context. A spokesman insisted the businessman-turned-politician would not be cowed by calls to withdraw or to censor his remarks, arguing that his appeal lay in challenging what he described as a “rigged system” and in speaking plainly to voters who feel left behind by the political establishment. The episode comes against a backdrop of upheaval within the Trump operation. It emerged late on Friday that one of his most senior political advisers had left the campaign, a departure that underscored the volatility surrounding his bid for the Republican nomination. People close to the operation described the exit as a personnel shift prompted by strategic disagreements and the intense scrutiny that accompanies a high-profile front-runner, rather than a sign of an imminent collapse. The campaign emphasised there was no rift that would derail its operations, but acknowledged that staff churn has become a recurring feature since the campaign began to coalesce around a broader campaign strategy. Within hours of CPAC’s announcement, a chorus of criticism from lawmakers and commentators intensified. Critics argued that Mr Trump’s rhetoric risked alienating women voters, a demographic data point the Republican field has long sought to win over in a general election. Supporters, by contrast, argued that the remarks were blown out of proportion and that the real issue for voters remained the economy, security, and national leadership. Megyn Kelly, the Fox News anchor who challenged Mr Trump during the earlier debate, did not respond directly to the latest turn of events. Her colleagues and representatives reiterated that she would keep pursuing questions on policy and temperament from all candidates in the race. The exchange and its fallout have become a prominent reminder of how the contest has fused entertainment, media combat and political campaigning in a way not seen in recent presidential races. Analysts emphasised that CPAC’s decision would deprive Mr Trump of a highly visible platform to articulate his case to conservative activists at a moment when his campaign has sought to reinvigorate momentum after a difficult stretch. It also highlighted the fragility of the alliances that propel front-runners within the party, where endorsements, speaking slots and networks of influence can swiftly shift the trajectory of a campaign. As the weekend closes, campaign aides say Mr Trump will redirect his focus to upcoming events and interviews designed to showcase his policy positions and to rally his core base. The broader political climate, with the primaries still months away and the general election looming, remains uncertain, and this latest controversy is likely to be a defining talking point in the weeks ahead.

title: French intelligence agents are looking into a claim by al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb to have kidnapped seven foreign workers at a uranium mine in Niger.
text_ai: A statement purportedly by the militant group said it would issue demands to the French government "shortly" and warned it against "anything stupid". France has sent troops to hunt for the hostages, five of whom are French. The others are from Togo and Madagascar. Niger’s government said it was aware of the claim and was coordinating with French authorities and the mine’s operators to verify the report. A spokesman for the president told reporters that ministers were “following developments closely” and that no confirmation had yet been received about the identities or numbers of the workers. The government urged calm while security agencies conducted checks in the region, which has long seen jihadist activity and criminal trafficking. France said it was working with Niamey and the mine’s owner to locate the seven workers, and that its forces were aiding the search operation. The defence ministry described the situation as “a matter of high concern” and said Paris would provide intelligence and logistical support as long as it was needed. A French official refused to speculate on possible ransom demands or timing, stressing that any action would be guided by hostages’ safety. The workers are said to include five French nationals and two other nationals from Togo and Madagascar. The Arlit area in northern Niger, home to large-scale uranium mining, has long been a fragile security corridor where jihadist groups have exploited local grievances and monitoring gaps. The site is operated by a foreign-led consortium with state involvement, and the workers’ disappearance would be the most serious incident there in years. AQIM issued a brief statement last night claiming the seven captives had been seized “in connection with the French military escalation” in the Sahel and warning Paris against “any stupid move.” The authenticity of the claim could not immediately be established, and intelligence services have cautioned that such messages can be designed to test responses or distract from other operations. Niger’s security forces, backed by international partners, have stepped up patrols in border areas and around key infrastructure since last week’s clashes in the region. Analysts say the volatile mix of militant activity, trafficking networks, and poverty in parts of the Sahel makes hostage-taking in remote mining zones possible, though authorities emphasise that the likelihood of a successful operation remains uncertain. Humanitarian groups have urged restraint and access for aid workers if and when it becomes possible. International reaction has focused on supporting Niamey’s efforts while avoiding actions that could endanger the captives. The United Nations said it was monitoring the situation closely and urged all parties to protect civilians and adhere to international humanitarian law.
