Milik’s reaction suggested the weight of expectation on his shoulders, the frustration of not starting, and the relief of finally belonging in the action. “Bit by bit, we found our rhythm,” said Klaassen afterwards, voice taut but composed. “We kept believing. When you’ve got a striker like Milik on the pitch, you know you’ll get your chances. We just have to be more ruthless in the box.” Celtic responded with a flurry of pressing and short, quick passes that sought to pin Ajax back in their own half. Brown, in particular, orchestrated a shift of tempo, dropping into the space behind the midfield to collect the ball and drive through the lines. The home crowd, half an hour earlier subdued, found their voice again as the clock slipped into the final ten minutes. With eight minutes remaining, Milik finally found the moment for which Ajax had waited. Younes produced a cross from the left after another patient buildup, and Milik rose above the Celtic defence to plant a clean header past Gordon at the near post. The ball kissed the underside of the bar on its way in and dropped behind the stranded goalkeeper for a moment before rolling across the line. The Amsterdam ArenA erupted. The goal changed the tenor of the game. Celtic pushed higher, but Ajax protected their lead with a disciplined shape and compact lines, denying space in the middle and pressing the ball carrier with relentless intent. Gordon produced one more saves-from-danger moment, pushing a rising drive from Milik over the bar after a clever lay-off from Klaassen as the ball bobbed and wove its way back into the box. In the minutes that followed, Celtic introduced fresh legs, hoping to pin Ajax back in the dying embers of the evening. The tactic bore fruit only in a limited way, though, as the Dutch side tightened their grip and moved the ball with a maturity that suggested a team that had spent enough evenings grinding out results to know how to manage a late advantage in a European tie. When the final whistle sounded, there was a sense of relief in the Ajax dugout and a sense of quiet disappointment in Celtic’s bench. The home side had finally unlocked a stubborn barrier with a moment of clinical quality, while Celtic could feel they had done enough to question their opponent’s rhythm but not enough to force a draw that would have kept their campaign alive. “We can take the positives from tonight,” said a subdued Deila, Celtic’s manager, offering a measured assessment. “We created chances, and we defended well for long spells, but in Europe you need to take your moments when they come and we didn’t do that often enough. We’ll go again.” For Ajax, the result felt like control regained after a period of frustrating stalemate. Milik’s late contribution, in particular, provided the kind of proof-of-life moment the hosts needed to justify the decision to start him on the bench and then bring him into the game. The Polish striker, who had been a spark off the bench in a crucial European night before, had delivered with a composure that had the stands in a hush before his header and a roar after. As the players left the field, the air around the ArenA carried a familiar mix of relief and expectation. This is the league that tests nerve and finishes by insisting on precision. Ajax will travel to Celtic Park with a slender advantage and a collection of lessons learned about keeping the tempo relentless, about turning pressure into a decisive breakthrough, and about the fine line between frustration and fulfilment on a European night.

title: In the Disney Pixar animation The Incredibles, the daughter in the family of superheroes, Violet, has a particular superpower.
text_ai: She can create a protective force field around herself - an impenetrable bubble. She can also make herself invisible. Businesses trying to ward off millions of dangerous cyber-attacks in an increasingly connected world probably wish they had the same superpower. Well, perhaps now, they do. In the real world, the idea is being marketed by a handful of firms that say they can deliver a digital force field around a company’s networks, data and devices. One London-based start-up, ShieldBubble, has rolled out a product it calls simply Bubble, pitched as an invisible shield for people, information and infrastructure. The company says it builds a real-time perimeter that moves with users and devices, regardless of whether they sit inside a corporate data centre or drift across hybrid clouds. Bubble relies on a few key ideas that have gained currency in security circles over the last decade: zero-trust networking, continuous verification, micro-segmentation and pervasive encryption. In practice, that means every attempt to access a file or an application is checked, every device and user is given a dynamic, minimal set of permissions, and nothing is allowed to travel freely unless it has passed those checks again and again. Experts say the approach flips the conventional model on its head. Rather than fortress-like perimeters that assume everyone inside is trustworthy, a dynamic shield assumes compromise is possible and seeks to limit what an intruder can do once inside. The result, proponents argue, is not an impenetrable wall but a difficult maze that slows attackers and buys time for the defender to respond. Analysts caution that no technology is a panacea. Dr Ava Singh, a cyber risk researcher at the Royal Institute of Digital Security, saysBubble-like systems can dramatically reduce the window in which a breach can spread, but they cannot prevent breaches from happening entirely. “What you are buying is containment with better visibility,” she says. “It’s about reducing dwell time and restricting lateral movement within an environment, which is where the damage tends to occur.” For many organisations, the appeal lies as much in practicality as protection. Modern enterprises increasingly operate in hybrid environments where data and applications live in multiple clouds, on-premises facilities and partner networks. A transparent, adaptive shield can, in theory, apply consistent security policies across all those layers without requiring a complete architecture overhaul. Companies that have experimented with Bubble or similar technology say the benefits can be measurable but sometimes gradual. A multinational retailer that has piloted the system reports fewer alerts about non-critical anomalies after a staged rollout, along with a clearer view of who is accessing what and when. Their security team has welcomed the ability to quarantine a device or user with a few clicks, rather than having to unplug an entire segment of the network. The market for these technologies is being buoyed by a couple of longer-term trends. First, cybercriminals are broadening their attack surfaces. The shift to remote work, the expansion of cloud services and the growth of interconnected operational technology in sectors like utilities and manufacturing create more potential entry points. Second, regulators around the world are tightening requirements for breach notification, data handling and vendor risk management. Governments are urging organisations to adopt more robust access controls and to assume adversaries are already inside the network, deliberately or otherwise. Industry observers say adoption is likely to be uneven, reflecting differences in sector needs and budgets. Financial services firms, health providers and critical infrastructure operators arguably have the strongest incentive to invest heavily in advanced protections, given the high potential costs of breaches and the regulatory penalties that can follow. Small and medium-sized enterprises, meanwhile, may prioritise simpler, more cost-effective options or seek shared-security services offered by managed service providers. “Incremental improvements are common in this space,” says Rajiv Mistry, a cybersecurity strategist who advises several mid-sized European firms. “A lot of companies are still weighing whether they can justify the disruption and cost of a full zero-trust deployment against the risk the breach poses. The answer is usually a hybrid approach: keep your existing tools but layer in this kind of dynamic shield where it matters most.” The push comes as public and private sectors alike face a worrying surge in cyber incidents. In many cases, breaches begin with relatively banal footholds—phishing emails that lead to compromised credentials, misconfigured cloud storage, or software vulnerabilities that can be exploited without sophisticated exploits. When such breaches occur, speed of response becomes critical, and the ability to isolate parts of the network is often decisive in limiting damage. Critics, however, point to the practical challenges of deploying what is essentially a real-time governance layer across a sprawling and often legacy-heavy IT estate. They warn that security must be balanced with performance, privacy and the day-to-day needs of employees who rely on fast, reliable access to data and services. If the filters and checks are too aggressive, employees can experience bottlenecks that undermine productivity or push them toward workarounds that undermine the very protections the shield is intended to provide. Industry watchdogs also stress the importance of governance and transparency. With technologies that monitor users and devices so closely, there is a legitimate concern about how data is processed, stored and used. The privacy implications of deep, continuous monitoring will need to be addressed alongside any promised security benefits, they say. In the United Kingdom, the National Cyber Security Centre has long emphasised a layered approach to security that combines technology with strong governance and skilled people. In policy circles, there is broad acceptance that modern cyber defence must be able to contend with a small army of increasingly capable attackers, many of whom operate with the intent of ransom, espionage or disruption. That has prompted calls for more standardised procurement of security components and better information-sharing between companies and government. No matter the specific configuration, the emerging consensus is that the battlefield has shifted. The goal, as many security leaders describe it, is to render a cyberattack more costly and time-consuming for the intruder while enabling defenders to act with greater speed and certainty. The “bubble” metaphor has become more than a marketing slogan in this regard; it is a way of reframing what an enterprise needs to survive in a world where digital systems are no longer a nice-to-have but a critical operating backbone. As for Violet’s fictional bubble, security professionals say it serves as a useful reminder that protection in the modern age is as much about policy, people and processes as it is about devices and software. The best shields, they argue, are layered and intelligent—designed to adapt to evolving threats, while remaining mindful of the human work that keeps organisations secure. Whether Bubble or its competitors ultimately deliver a widely adopted standard remains to be seen. What is clear is that the concept of an ever-present, adaptive shield—capable of rotating through policies and isolating threats in real time—reflects a broader industry shift: away from a single firewall at the edge, toward a living, responsive architecture that travels with the user and the data across every corner of the digital domain. In a world where the next breach could be a matter of when, not if, organisations everywhere are weighing how best to armour themselves without losing sight of the people, the markets and the information they protect.

title: Chancellor of the Exchequer Philip Hammond was on the BBC's Breakfast programme on Thursday, talking about the changes made in his Budget.
text_ai: The claim: 60% of self-employed people will pay less National Insurance as a result of these changes. Reality Check verdict: 60% of people according to Treasury estimates will pay less, but only if you combine the abolition of Class 2 National Insurance contributions, which was announced in 2016, with the increase in Class 4 contributions announced on Wednesday. The reality, as the Treasury itself acknowledges, is more nuanced than the headline figure suggests. The 60% headcount rests on a modelling approach that assumes the planned abolition of Class 2 National Insurance contributions and the specific increase in Class 4 NICs will be implemented as outlined. It also depends on earnings profiles across the self-employed population, from those with modest profits to those with much higher turnover. Class 2 is a small, flat-rate charge paid weekly by many self-employed workers. Abolishing it would, in isolation, cut their bills by a fixed sum, regardless of profits. By contrast, Class 4 is proportionate to profits and scales with earnings. The increase mooted on Wednesday would raise the rate on portions of profit, narrowing or reversing some of the gain that a straightforward abolition would yield for higher earners. Taken together, the Treasury says, these moves would tilt the balance in favour of most self-employed people, but only if both changes go ahead as planned. Finance ministers emphasised that the net effect will vary by sector and by the level of income. Those with the lowest profits, who would otherwise already be on the lower end of Class 4 contributions, stand to benefit from the removal of Class 2 but may see little extra relief from the higher Class 4 rate. High earners, meanwhile, could see a mixed picture: the removal of Class 2 helps, but the higher Class 4 rate could erode part of that gain. The Opposition seized on the numbers to argue that the Government was cooking the books or oversimplifying the impact on real lives. A Labour spokesperson said the Budget failed to deliver a fair deal for the self-employed, many of whom work on precarious margins and rely on clear, simple rules. They urged the Government to publish a more granular breakdown showing where the gains and losses would land for different groups. Tax experts also urged caution, noting that the NIC changes interact with other reforms and with welfare thresholds. For example, adjustments to universal credit, pension protections, and business reliefs could dampen or amplify the practical outcome for an individual self-employed worker. Mr Hammond, speaking on Breakfast, defended the package as a pragmatic step toward simplifying the system and backing small business. He argued that, taken as a package, the measures would encourage enterprise while ensuring a fair contribution from those with the greatest ability to pay. The Treasury said further analyses would be published in the autumn financial statement, with the numbers subject to change as policy design proceeds.

title: In the not-too-distant future, our fields could be tilled, sown, tended and harvested entirely by fleets of co-operating autonomous machines by land and air.
text_ai: And they'll be working both day and night. Driverless tractors that can follow pre-programmed routes are already being deployed at large farms around the world. Drones are buzzing over fields assessing crop health and soil conditions. Ground sensors are monitoring the amount of water and nutrients in the soil, triggering irrigation and fertiliser applications. Across regions as varied as the Netherlands, Texas and Queensland, fleets of autonomous wheel and wing are becoming ordinary features of the landscape. In large arable operations, coordinators talk of a “swarm” of machines that can share tasks, communicate breaches in a plan, and adapt in real time to weather shifts or weed outbreaks. Farmers describe a shift from daily micromanagement to overseeing systems and responding to alerts rather than walking every boundary. In trials and early commercial rollouts, driverless tractors are handling tasks from seeding to harvest aid, while drones map crop health and pests and deploy inputs with surgical precision. Ground-based robots survey row by row, using machine vision to identify stressed plants and dormant weeds. The data streams feed into control centres and to cloud platforms where algorithms forecast yield, regulate irrigation and fine-tune fertiliser applications. The ambition is not merely automation, but a reconfigurable farm that can switch crops, adjust to market signals, and optimise resource use with much less waste. Farmers are cautiously optimistic. “The first months were learning curves,” says Elena García, who manages a 2,000-hectare estate near Valencia that has begun integrating autonomous planters and aerial sprayers. “But once the machines understood our fields, the level of control you gain is extraordinary. You get alerts when a soil slab dries out, or when a nutrient deficiency appears before you see it with the naked eye.” Her sentiment is echoed by operators who say the systems reduce routine fatigue and free up human labour for tasks that require judgment, such as matching crop choices to climate forecasts or planning cover crops for soil health. Industry leaders point to a growing ecosystem of collaborating devices capable of long endurance and rapid decision making. Ground sensors are linked to irrigation rigs and fertigation systems, while drone fleets provide on-demand checks on plant density, canopy temperature and water stress. The technology is evolving toward “interfaces” that let a single operator supervise multiple sites, with the ability to pause, reroute or reassign machines via a smartphone or tablet. But the shift is not without questions. Regulators in several countries are evaluating the safety frameworks that will govern remote operation, collision avoidance, and the integrity of data collected across fields. A spokesperson for the European Commission said that while automation can boost resilience in farming, the rules governing autonomy, liability and data protection must keep pace with the technology so that farmers are not left bearing the costs of failures or breaches. The UK’s Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs has signalled a similar stance, emphasising risk assessment, cyber-security standards and transparent data governance. Cyber-security is a practical concern for many farm managers. In a sector where a single incursion could disrupt irrigation, pest control or harvest schedules, robust encryption, secure software updates and fail-safe modes are no longer optional. “The risk is not just about machines failing,” notes Dr Sara Patel, a safety engineer who specialises in agricultural robotics. “If someone can tamper with the control software, the whole system can be misdirected. The corridor between technology and food security is narrow and must be protected.” The cost question remains central, especially for smaller farms. While large estates move toward subscription models and shared service arrangements—where a central provider owns and maintains the fleet and farmers pay for access—smallholders worry about access, affordability and the potential for stranded assets. Analysts say that service-based approaches, modular hardware, and open-data standards could widen participation, but only if financing mechanisms and local training accompany rollout. In parts of Africa and Asia, where labour markets are tight and land tenure can be complex, policy makers are exploring public-private partnerships to fund pilots, provide affordable equipment leases and build local maintenance capacity. The environmental case for automation is often framed in terms of precision and conservation. When irrigation and fertiliser can be triggered on the basis of exact soil moisture and plant need, water use and chemical input can shrink. Early pilots have reported improvements in uniformity of application and reductions in runoff, with the added benefit of enabling crops to be managed under more complex rotation schemes that improve soil structure over time. Opponents caution that automation should not become an excuse to avoid farming practices that are inherently sustainable—such as soil amendment or crop diversification—if such strategies are not compatible with the system’s optimization criteria. Meanwhile, labour markets are adapting. Agri-tech firms say the deployment phase creates demand for technicians, data scientists and remote operators who can manage fleets, calibrate sensors and interpret analytics. In rural areas, community colleges and training providers are expanding curricula to cover robotics, automation maintenance and data literacy for agriculture. Farmers who once spent hours in the cab are finding new roles in overseeing algorithms, auditing results and coordinating with agronomists to adjust the system’s parameters to local conditions. There is also a broader social dimension to consider. The rapid adoption of autonomous farming tools raises questions about data ownership and control. Who owns the field data generated by sensors, drone imagery and vehicle telemetry? How is this data shared, sold or anonymised? Industry bodies and several national regulators are beginning to draft guidelines on data stewardship to ensure farmers retain ownership of information about their land and practices, while allowing producers of the technology to improve their products. In the field, voices from farming communities are mixed. Some farmers say automation helps them stay competitive in an environment of volatile input costs and climatic stress. Others fear being edged out by the latest machine or by a system that makes all the decisions from afar, with scant room for human intuition—especially in the early morning hours when anomalies appear and the workload spikes. For many, the answer lies in a hybrid approach: automation where it makes sense, human oversight where context and nuance matter. As the pace of change accelerates, the next decade could redefine what “the farm” looks like. Fields may be crisscrossed by lines of autonomous machines, every inch monitored and managed, yet still needing the human eye to interpret weather signals, market signals and the long view of soil and biodiversity. The BBC spoke to several farming families who emphasise that technology is a tool, not a replacement for knowledge and care for the land. In a small greenhouse in rural Ontario, a manager shows a tablet screen displaying a map of a crop cycle. A drone circles above; a ground robot trundles along the row. On the screen, a forecast model adjusts irrigation timing for the next 24 hours. The system flags a potential nutrient imbalance in a patch of soil and suggests a targeted application, a suggestion that can be executed automatically or paused for human review. The manager nods slowly. “Automation has given us new hands to work with,” she says, “hands that never tire, that can monitor dozens of fields at once. But the wisdom in the field—what the crop needs, what it can tolerate, what the weather will do—still comes from people who know the land.”

title: Ched Evans should be allowed to play football again when he is released from prison, says Professional Footballers' Association chief Gordon Taylor.

title: India's restive Jammu and Kashmir state is again facing crisis following the death of chief minister Mufti Mohammad Sayeed on 7 January.

title: Indian leaders must sometimes have felt a little overwhelmed when they arrived in Brussels.
text_ai: India has always been the poor relation in economic terms and more often than not the question has been how Europe - that great union of some of the richest and most powerful countries in the modern world - can help India. Officials emphasised that the region’s authorities remain committed to collaborating with national partners, business leaders, and community groups to secure the best possible use of EU funds, whatever the final algorithm may be. Brussels is expected to publish its final grant allocations later in the year.

title: It has been a tradition since the days of Winston Churchill that the prime minister's address at the annual Lord Mayor's Banquet in London is devoted to foreign policy.
text_ai: For the past four years David Cameron has argued that the bed-rock of this should be economic self-interest - Britain's foreign policy needed a new "hard headed" commercial focus, to seek out new trade and investment partners round the world. Among those new partners was Russia. The brief in the Guildhall that night was not one of sermonising or moral warning, but of diplomacy dressed in a business suit. As drum rolls faded and the City’s red banners glittered under chandeliers, Mr Cameron’s audience sat ready for the message he has settled on as his guiding principle: export, invest, build alliances, and let Britain’s economy pull foreign policy along in its wake. In the first moments of his address, the Prime Minister telegraphed the shift that has characterised his approach since entering office. “What we need is a foreign policy that is not merely about values and principles in the abstract, but about real waking-after-the-dawn consequences for jobs, for businesses and for the British people,” he told the room, drawing a line that critics would say was both pragmatic and blunt. “We must be hard-headed about our national interests, and we must be ambitious for Britain’s economy.” That insistence on economic self-interest as the engine of diplomacy has, for four years, been Cameron’s refrain. And within that refrain lay the thrust of tonight’s message: Britain should be courting new markets around the world, and that includes cultivating relationships with nations that once seemed distant or even incompatible with Britain’s traditional allies. Russia, Cameron argued, was not merely a source of energy or a potential market for goods; it was, he suggested, a country whose modernisation and reform could be accelerated by Britain’s expertise in financial services, infrastructure, and services. The PM’s rhetorical pivot was easy to hear in the talk that rippled through the room as the speech moved from abstract principles to concrete opportunities. Britain, he said, would seek out “new partners for a new century,” not as a retreat from Europe or a betrayal of allied values, but as a strategic necessity in a world where economic influence translates into political levers and security guarantees. In that sense, the urban myth of the “global Britain” he has long championed took on a sharper, more transactional edge. Within minutes of the opening, though, the room’s mood began to shift as Cameron turned to one of the most delicate parts of his thesis: managing relations with Russia. He spoke of Russia as “a country with vast potential” but framed that potential within the context of sanctions, international norms, and the rule of law. Acknowledging the concerns of many in the room, he insisted that Britain would keep “a clear line” on human rights and on Moscow’s activities in Ukraine and elsewhere. Yet he argued that even in the face of such concerns, economic engagement—properly measured and properly governed—could still be part of a broader policy that sought to stabilise markets and foster constructive dialogue. The business chiefs present welcomed the shift in rhetoric, at least in its emphasis on opportunity. The City has long played a double game in relation to Russia: one eye on the potential for profit from Russian capital, and another on the geopolitical risks that come with dealing with a state that has shown itself unpredictable at times. A senior executive from a major London-based financial services firm said afterwards that the real test would be what concrete measures followed the speech. “Talk is cheap,” he said, “but investment follows certainty. If the government can provide a clear pathway—through regulatory clarity, a predictable tax framework for long-term investment, and a robust sanctions regime that still allows legitimate trade—then London will remain the preferred hub for Russian capital.” The UK’s bid to deepen ties with Russia has not always sat neatly with the policy line taken by some of Britain’s European allies. In debates inside Parliament and in the days of the Crimea crisis that would soon sharpen the sense of Europe’s unity, Cameron’s team argued that diversification of markets should not come at the expense of Europe. William Hague, the Foreign Secretary, told journalists that Britain would not renounce its commitments to international law or its close ties with the European Union while pursuing a more ambitious global economic strategy. “We must keep our options open,” he said, “and we must be prepared to work with all responsible partners, but never, ever sacrifice our standards or our obligations.” Not all who heard the Prime Minister that evening were persuaded. Labour’s foreign affairs spokesperson warned that turning foreign policy into a ledger of potential profits risked blurring the line between statecraft and commercial opportunism. “There is a danger in becoming dependent on the very markets we depend on to mete out restraint,” he said in a later interview. “If foreign policy is simply about sales and contracts, we risk forfeiting credibility on the world stage when risks become uncomfortable.” The shadow argument sharpened as Cameron’s speech wandered into a section about sanctions and the need for a coherent, coalition-driven response to any violation of international norms. The Prime Minister argued that economic diplomacy and sanctions could act in tandem: “When the time calls for penalties, we must be ready to act, but we must also be ready to offer a credible economic path back to stability for those involved.” The balance, he suggested, would be France, Germany, and Britain standing together with a united front, and with the United States playing its role as a near partner in both strategy and support. In the corridors outside the Grand Hall, talk focused as much on timing as on content. Some said Cameron’s speech was a recognition that the political world has grown messy and that business could no longer pretend it existed in a vacuum. Others warned that the risks of engaging with Moscow—intelligence concerns, the potential for reputational damage, and the complex legalities of sanctions—were real and not easily outweighed by short-term commercial gain. The sheer scale of capital and resource links between Britain and Russia had to be managed with ironclad governance and transparent oversight, they argued, lest a misstep undermine decades of careful economic diplomacy. Amid the debate, other voices offered a broader historical lens. Several veteran Moscow-watchers reminded the room that Britain had pursued engagement with Russia since the late 1990s, with a mix of optimism and caution shaped by the ebb and flow of Russian reform and Western policy. They noted that Russia’s economy, heavily dependent on energy and state-driven enterprises, could be a powerful partner or a fragile one, depending on the political weather and the international rules that governed trade and investment. The City’s mood, while optimistic about opportunity, also carried a note of restraint. There was impatience with the bureaucratic frictions that could slow even the most promising deals, and a recognition that sanctions regimes, despite Cameron’s assurances, added a layer of risk for lenders and investors. A banker who has spent two decades navigating London’s relationships with Moscow pointed to a paradox at the heart of Cameron’s argument: the very openness Britain claims to champion is what makes it necessary to maintain the most disciplined risk controls and compliance regimes when dealing with Russian counterparties. As the night wore on, Cameron pivoted to another pillar of his agenda: trade and investment not as mere adjuncts to diplomacy, but as engines of security. He sketched out a plan for a new slate of trade missions—well-organised, well-funded, and backed by ministers moving in lockstep with the City’s clubs and chambers of commerce. The aim, he said, was not to prod a reluctant market into submission but to cultivate a climate in which British firms could compete on fair terms, backed by legal certainty, robust dispute resolution, and a transparent framework for property rights and taxation. The closing notes reiterated the Government’s long-term strategy: to position Britain as a global hub where capital, ideas, and talent could move freely. It was, Cameron argued, about “open societies and open markets,” a line that has become a comfort blanket for supporters of his policy and a sticking point for opponents who worry about the moral compromises such openness might entail. Outside the Guildhall’s doors, the city’s rain-slick streets reflected the contrast between policy and practice. The same city that had learned to live with the volatility of global finance would be watching closely how Cameron’s new emphasis on economic diplomacy translated into real outcomes: a translation that could, in the weeks and months ahead, redraw the contours of Britain’s international role. If the Prime Minister’s speech tonight offered a reframing of foreign policy as a function of the economy, it also set a test for the government: could it pursue a more assertive global presence without sacrificing the principles that, in theory, define Britain’s place in the world? The answer, for the moment, lay in the details—of contracts signed, of sanctions complied with, of disputes resolved, and of a City that would not merely tolerate, but actively enable, a more expansive and sometimes uncomfortable global footprint. The Lord Mayor’s Banquet might be a ceremonial stage, but Cameron’s words were real policy bait—a signal that Britain, in a time of global flux, would try to walk a line between profit and principle, diplomacy and markets, assertiveness and alliance. And whether those lines would prove sustainable remained a question that would be answered not in the glow of an evening’s applause but in the months to come, as ministers, negotiators, and businessmen carried the vision forward into the world’s markets.

title: Ofcom is to investigate whether viewers were duped into voting for a stunt dog in the final of Britain's Got Talent.
text_ai: The broadcasting watchdog received 1,150 complaints after trainer Jules O'Dwyer used a second dog to perform a tightrope walk because her Border Collie, Matisse, was afraid of heights. ITV boss Peter Fincham later admitted the programme should have made it clear that a different dog was used. Ofcom confirmed it has opened a formal investigation into whether the finale misled viewers into voting for a dog act that did not feature the animal named in the act’s billing. The watchdog said it would assess whether the programme presented the performance in a way that could be considered deceptive, and whether on-screen material or host commentary sufficiently disclosed the substitution. The 1,150 complaints followed the finale, with dozens of viewers arguing that the public vote had been influenced by a lack of transparency about which dog actually performed the tightrope routine. Ofcom said its inquiry would look at all episodes of the show that contributed to the final, including any pre-publicity, social media posts and post-broadcast promotion. .ITV said it would fully cooperate with the regulator and stressed that it had acted in good faith throughout the series. A spokesperson added: “We recognise the concerns raised and will assist Ofcom with its assessment. The safety and welfare of animals are a priority for ITV, and we will review our on-screen messaging to ensure clarity for viewers.” Jules O’Dwyer herself has previously defended the act, saying the second dog was used to complete the routine after her first dog’s fear of heights made the stunt impractical. Her representatives have argued that the audience saw a two-dog routine on screen and that viewers were never misled about the core concept of the act. The case raises broader questions about how talent shows describe animal acts and whether disclosures about substitutions should appear during the broadcast or only in the programme’s end credits. Ofcom warned that it would publish its findings and, if necessary, outline remedies or sanctions for any breaches of the broadcasting code. A date for the preliminary ruling has not been set.

title: Councils have welcomed an increase in the amount of money the government plans to give them in the coming year - but few are celebrating.
text_ai: Critics argue councils will still get less government money than this year which they actually have control over. The government agreed a budget deal yesterday to give councils £160 million more than previously planned. Councils are now working out just what impact this will have on their own finances. The extra funding comes as ministers insist the money is not a blank cheque, but a recognition that local authorities are grappling with spiralling costs as demand for care and homelessness support grows. Officials said the £160m uplift was designed to be spread across the country to help cash-strapped councils keep services running, rather than to fund any specific new programmes. How much any one council will receive will depend on a range of factors, including population, the age profile of residents and pressures in social care and housing. Reaction from council leaders was mixed. Some said the injection would provide a needed buffer as they begin year-end pressures and prepare for next year’s budgets. One leader from a large northern authority called the move “a small but welcome step” that would help with winter resilience and frontline services. But others warned that the money would not reverse years of tight funding and rising demand. A spokesperson for the Local Government Association said the settlement gave councils “breathing space” but added that longer-term, predictable funding was what was required to avoid repeated last-minute budget gaps. “Councils are not asking for a blank cheque,” they said. “They are asking for stability and the ability to plan for the growing needs of their communities.” Officials emphasised that the extra cash would not, on its own, fix every problem facing local services. Critics point to the fact that while the £160m is a positive development, it sits on top of a wider package that has already left many authorities with limited headroom for the next decade. Inflation, energy costs and wage settlements for care staff continue to bite, and demand for adult social care, children’s services and homelessness support remains stubbornly high. Analysts note that the distribution method means some councils will see a relatively modest uplift per resident, while others with acute pressures may use the funds to shore up social care or temporary accommodation costs. In regions where populations are expanding quickly or where needs are highest, the impact could be more pronounced, say observers. The government’s position remains that the money is part of a broader reform of local government funding aimed at giving councils more control over their own tax-raising powers while ensuring essential services are protected. Ministers say the settlement is designed to give councils the space to plan for the coming year with a little more certainty. For now, many councils will be crunching the numbers, weighing up potential increases to council tax in their area against the need to protect vulnerable residents. The true test, as ever, will be how the extra cash translates into front-line services for people in towns and cities across the country.

title: Of all the frustrations that a broken ankle brings, it is missing life at Firhill that is paining David Beattie most.

title: Often the simplest questions are the hardest to answer.
text_ai: As we reported yesterday, the troubles of the inquiry into historical child abuse continue to unravel. title: It was a case that shattered confidence in the British legal system, sparked an Oscar-winning film and eventually an apology from a prime minister.
text_ai: Some thought when Tony Blair apologised to Gerry Conlon, Paddy Armstrong, Paul Hill and Carole Richardson, it drew a line under one of the most scarring episodes of the Troubles in Northern Ireland. For those who lived through the long wake of those convictions, the meeting between a housed-in justice system and a small group of ordinary people felt less like vindication than a fragile pause in a national reckoning with the state’s reach. The Guildford Four, named after the Surrey town where the bombs tore through two packed pubs in October 1974, spent years locked inside a narrative that appeared to fit the political weather — that fierce, sometimes secret war against the IRA required harsh measures. What followed was a sequence of events that would reverberate far beyond their lives: confessions, a trial, a sentence that seemed to fit a terror campaign, a film starved of nuance and a public increasingly prepared to question whether the core of the justice system could ever be trusted again. When the Court of Appeal quashed their convictions in 1989, it did more than set four men free. It jolted a nation into reconsidering what law officers could and could not do in the name of law and order. The Guildford Four became emblematic, not just of a miscarriage, but of a pattern of miscarriages that would later prompt far-reaching reform. The release was greeted with a mixture of relief and a silent fear: what did it say about the people who had watched them suffer, and about the methods used to secure convictions in a climate of fear? That fear fed a cultural response as much as a legal one. The Oscar-winning film In the Name of the Father, based on Gerry Conlon’s story and produced with the voices of those around him, brought to a broader audience the human cost of a miscarriage of justice. It portrayed a nation wrestling with the idea that the police and security services, in trying to defeat violence, might taint the very process designed to protect citizens. The film’s reach helped keep public attention on the case at a moment when memory of the Troubles remained raw, and it solidified the Guildford Four’s place in the national conscience as more than just a footnote in the history books. In the years after the quashing, the state acknowledged that a wrong had been done — a conclusion that arrived, slowly, through the language of apologies, compensation and the dawning realisation that British justice had to grow beyond the era of blanket emergency measures. Tony Blair, then prime minister, publicly acknowledged the harm caused to the four men and their families. His apology did not erase what had happened, but it did mark a formal recognition that the state had fallen short of the standards it should have upheld. For many, the apology was a necessary step toward a broader, institutional reckoning with how miscarriages occur and what must be done to prevent them in the future. Crucially, the Guildford Four’s case helped catalyse structural change in the system. Rushed trials, heavily relied-upon confessional evidence, and insufficient safeguards for the innocent were thrust into the spotlight. The creation of the Criminal Cases Review Commission, established in 1997, was among the most tangible reforms. The commission was designed to provide a fresh, independent look at potential miscarriages at a living stage long after trials had ended, offering a route to revisit convictions on grounds of new evidence or new doubts about the fairness of proceedings. It was not a cure-all — no reform is — but it signalled a shift in how Britain approached justice, acknowledging that errors can and do occur, and that the state has a duty to correct them. Yet the story does not end with legal mechanics and official apologies. For many families, and for supporters to this day, there remains a stubborn sense that justice, while partly restored, never fully healed the wounds inflicted during those years. Questions persist about the relationships between police investigations and political pressures, about the extent to which security concerns can be balanced with civil liberties, and about what more could have been done to prevent a miscarriage from taking root in the first place. The lives of Gerry Conlon, Paddy Armstrong, Paul Hill and Carole Richardson — and the lives of their relatives — were altered forever by an episode that, to this day, serves as a touchstone in debates about civil liberties and state accountability. Supporters argue that the fight for justice did not end with the relief of release or even with the government’s formal contrition. They point to continuing calls for a thorough, independent inquiry into the conduct of the police investigation, the handling of evidence, and the possible involvement of security services in the circumstances surrounding the case. They emphasise that a true reckoning requires more than a settlement and a public apology; it requires a careful, transparent examination of what happened, and why, so that lessons can be applied to current and future cases. In this sense, the Guildford Four’s legacy is a living argument for ongoing vigilance in the justice system, a reminder that the past still casts a long shadow over the present. The argument has never been simply about a single, painful chapter in the Troubles. It has been about the integrity of institutions, about the power of the state to shape narratives under pressure, and about the moral obligation to protect the innocent even when doing so complicates the fight against violence. For those who lived through it, the period carries a layered memory: relief at personal freedom, anger at the manner in which that freedom was compromised, and an insistence that history’s memory should not fade into quiet acceptance. The memory is not a single story but a chorus of voices — the Four themselves, their families, journalists who covered the case, legal scholars who have studied it, and ordinary people who found in the case a reason to demand more from those entrusted with power. What happened in Guildford also sits alongside a broader global story about miscarriages of justice in the late 20th century. The Birmingham Six, another group whose convictions were overturned in the same era, became part of a shared narrative that led to reforms across criminal justice systems in many democracies. The idea that a state could, under the pressures of terrorism, adopt investigative shortcuts or allow evidence to be misrepresented, destabilised public confidence in what should be the most secure of public processes. The Guildford Four’s case helped to propel reforms designed to reduce the risk of such miscarriages in the future: strengthened procedural protections for suspects, improved disclosure of material to defence teams, and more rigorous oversight of interrogations and confessions. The aim was not to undermine the state’s duty to protect citizens but to ensure that such protection remains consistent with the rule of law and human rights. As scholars and commentators look back, the case is frequently used as a cautionary tale about the human vulnerability at the center of the justice system. It reminds juries, judges, prosecutors, and police that the pursuit of security cannot eclipse the fundamental rights that underpin a fair trial. It also raises difficult questions about how the state should respond when mistakes are uncovered. Some argue that apologising publicly and offering compensation, while essential, must be accompanied by a candid inquiry into the processes that produced the miscarriages in the first place. Only through openness, they say, can trust be rebuilt and the public’s confidence in the law be restored. Those conversations are not merely historical. In recent years, they have fed into ongoing debates about how best to safeguard the rights of the accused in an era when counter-terrorism measures remain a significant political and legal issue. Proponents of stronger protections argue that the Guildford case demonstrates what can go wrong when speed and political necessity overshadow careful, principled practice. Critics of reform, meanwhile, warn against measures that they say risk hampering police work or compromising national security. The challenge for democracies is to navigate these tensions without repeating the missteps of the past. Within the Guildford Four’s circle, there is also the enduring question of how far justice extends to those who have been harmed by the miscarriage, and what constitutes real closure after so much time. For the families, the road to healing has often meant public validation, small acts of recognition, and a continuous demand that lessons from the past shape present and future policy. It has meant, too, celebrating small victories — the release from prison, the legal rulings that overturned convictions, the acknowledgement of wrongs — while living with the ongoing consequences of a long, arduous process that has touched communities far beyond Guildford. In that wider frame, the case has become a fixture in debates about the Troubles’ legacy and how to reconcile a history of violence with a modern, rights-based approach to justice. Northern Ireland’s own journey through decades of conflict has been marked by steps toward peace, but those steps have always been connected to and complicated by events elsewhere in the United Kingdom where the security state and the courts intersected in controversial ways. The Guildford Four’s story is thus not a solely domestic narrative but part of a broader conversation about how democracies remember, apologise, compensate, and reform after grievous errors. It is a reminder that the cost of error is paid not just by those who suffer directly but by the society that allows such errors to occur. Today, some still argue that a fuller truth should be sought, and that the public deserves a more thorough accounting of the case’s handling. Others stress the relative gains that reforms have brought, arguing that the system has learned to do better — not perfectly, but with a more robust framework for scrutinising convictions and ensuring the rights of the accused are protected at every stage. These are not abstract debates; the people at their heart — Gerry Conlon’s family, Paddy Armstrong’s relatives, Carole Richardson and Paul Hill’s loved ones, and the many others who believed their stories — remain the best witnesses to what went wrong and what needs to change. The story also has a cultural dimension that continues to resonate. The film’s enduring reach, its awards, and its narrative power helped keep the case in the public imagination long after the headlines moved on. It provided a lens through which audiences could question not only the actions of a few individuals within a complex system but the system itself — its incentives, its pressures, and its blind spots. The arts, in this sense, did what legal reforms alone could not: they humanised the consequences of a miscarriage, making it harder for the public to accept a tidy, impersonal explanation for why people were deprived of years of their lives. In the years since the apologies and the reforms, the public conversation around miscarriages of justice has evolved. The legal profession, media, and civil society have engaged in a continuous process of learning and accountability. There is now greater emphasis on the speed and quality of investigations, the consistent disclosure of exculpatory material, and the creation of safe spaces for whistleblowers and insiders who might challenge flawed procedures. The aim is not simply to prevent repeats of past errors but to foster a culture in which justice is actively protected, even in times of political strain. For the Guildford Four themselves, and for those who supported them, the journey has been a long one, marked by small steps toward recognition and large leaps of faith toward a more just system. They did not escape the shadow of what happened; rather, they carried it with them, turning it into a platform from which to argue for reform and for a more humane approach to those who have been accused of crimes in extraordinary circumstances. The memory of their years behind bars continues to shape how some lawyers, victims’ groups and policymakers think about how best to balance security with human rights. As Britain continues to reflect on its legal and political past, the Guildford Four’s story remains a reference point, not a relic. It is cited in classrooms, in policy debates, and in the countless legal cases that draw counsel from a shared history of accountability and reform. The case has become part of the national vocabulary when discussing the tension between state power and individual rights, when debating the adequacy of investigations, and when considering how best to repair trust after a grave error. In that sense, the fight for justice, albeit transformed, endures — not as a single battle won or lost, but as an ongoing effort to ensure that the line between safeguarding the public and preserving the rights of the individual remains clearly drawn, and forever watched by a vigilant public. For now, the memory of those turbulent years is carried by those who lived through them and by the generations that study the episodes in search of answers and remedies. The public institutions that learned from the Guildford Four’s case continue to face scrutiny, to defend their own legitimacy, and to remind themselves why transparency and accountability are not optional add-ons to the law but foundational requirements. If the last word in this chapter of British justice is still being written, it is being written with notes of humility, redress, and a renewed commitment to the principle that the innocent must never be sacrificed to expediency again. The Guildford Four’s story, in all its painful detail, remains a steady test of that promise.

title: Crews have taken a first look inside the Hoegh Osaka cargo ship, which had run aground in the Solent.
text_ai: The Hoegh Osaka was towed to Berth 101 at Southampton docks by four tugs, from a point between East Cowes and Lee-on-the-Solent, on Thursday. Opening the rear door on Friday revealed one of the pieces of heavy machinery it had been carrying. A small army of salvage workers, surveyors and coastguard officials stood by as the stern hatch, opened on Friday, admitted a narrow slice of the ship’s interior to daylight. Inside, a yellow wheeled excavator lay on its side among a tangle of steel frames and tarpaulins, its tracks caked with salt and mud. A crane hook dangled from the ceiling, and racks of pallets and cases were stacked in tight aisles, many secured with ratchet straps. The first inventory began with the visible items, while others were hidden behind the wreckage and darkness. The operation has been described as precautionary. A spokesman for the Maritime and Coastguard Agency said the priority was safety and containment, not exploitation of the cargo. “There is no indication of any fuel leakage at this stage,” the official said, though teams were prepared for any contingency and ready to deploy booms if needed. The ship’s rudder and hull appeared intact in the initial checks, but divers are expected to scrutinise the structure further in the coming days. Port authorities emphasised that it was too early to determine the full extent of the cargo survey, and that the vessel’s manifest would guide the focus of the inspection. The haul, they added, comprises a mix of vehicles and heavy equipment, all of it secured to prevent movement in rough seas. A team from the shipowner, Höegh Autoliner, accompanied the salvage operation to assist with the on-site accounting. Coastguard and port officials said there was no immediate threat to the shoreline or the Solent’s busy lanes, though they cautioned that the incident would be watched closely as tides shift and weather can change. The operation to survey, secure and eventually re-float the Osaka is expected to continue over the weekend, with a plan to re-deploy the vessel to a heavier-lift berth once the cargo is stabilised and the weather allows. Further updates are anticipated as surveys progress.

title: It was the discovery of a lifetime, an audacious Indiana Jones-style story of daring diving that uncovered a 400-year-old long-lost haul of Spanish treasure.
text_ai: When Belgian Robert Sténuit discovered pieces of eight in the murky, freezing seabed off Northern Ireland's north coast 50 years ago he knew he'd finally found it. Gold and artefacts deposited at the resting place of one of the most important ships in the Spanish Armada - the Girona. Decades of patient work since then have built a story far bigger than a single glittering heap. What researchers found this week, tucked beneath the cold, silty seabed in a sheltered shelf off the north coast, adds a new chapter to the Armada saga and to Northern Ireland’s underwater heritage. The expedition, a collaboration between the National Museums NI and a consortium led by the Belfast-based diving charity Atlantic Deep, was sanctioned after months of painstaking planning and diplomatic negotiations. The wreck, long understood to be the Girona’s resting place, has been treated as a protected site since the 1980s. But with modern underwater surveying techniques, the team said it could be studied without compromising conservation goals. An initial survey confirmed a secondary cache of artefacts—a haul that appears to have lain separate from the main cargo, possibly intended for a different consignment or destined for local markets along the route from Santander to the north Atlantic routes. Among the items recovered were hundreds of silver and copper coins minted in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, a cluster of gold ingots, and a surprising assemblage of smaller cargo items that include navigational instruments, a compass rose, a brass astrolabe fragment, and fittings from a shipment chest that would have protected its contents during storm and struggle. “The significance of this find stretches beyond the glitter,” said Dr. Isobel Hart, maritime archaeologist at the National Museums NI. “The coins help us date the voyage with unprecedented precision, and the artefacts illuminate the day-to-day realities of long-sea voyages in the late Elizabethan era—how sailors stored their wealth, what navigators trusted to guide them, and how cargo was prepared for the unpredictable Atlantic.” The team emphasised that the haul’s recovery was conducted with strict adherence to international and local heritage laws. Every artefact is being catalogued, photographed, and photographed again under controlled lab conditions before safe conservation is considered. The researchers say the majority will be preserved in situ until they can be moved to a purpose-built facility designed to stabilise metals that have lain in seawater for centuries. Officials acknowledged the emotional and economic weight of the discovery. The Girona’s treasure has long fed public imagination, symbolising the perilous reach of the Armada and the reckless gamble of treasure ships that sailed into English waters in search of fortune. Yet the scientific returns could be as important as the financial one. The coins, the inscriptions on the religious medals, and the style of the cargo chests offer a window into the networks that supplied the fleet—networks that crossed from the Iberian Peninsula into Ireland and onward into Atlantic shipping lanes that connected markets across Europe and the Americas. So far, analysts have been able to confirm a warren of small casks and tie-downs, still sealed after all these years, along with a handful of intact or near-intact ingots. The surface of some coins bears mint marks that scholars say will allow a much more detailed reconstruction of where the Girona’s cargo was intended to end up and who financed its voyage. The Girona’s story is intrinsically linked to those of the sailors who manned it—a crew that faced not only the risk of weather and enemy ships but the constant threat of shipworm damage, shifting currents, and the cold that could drain a person’s strength in minutes. For descendants of seafaring families in Northern Ireland and across the Irish Sea, the discovery is a reminder of a shared maritime history—one that contains both danger and opportunity. Legal questions continue to shadow the find. The Protection of Wrecks Act 1973 and subsequent legislation govern who may recover artefacts from protected wrecks and who may own them. In recent years, the UK and Northern Ireland have stressed a policy of shared stewardship—ensuring that recoveries serve education and research, with artefacts returning to public institutions rather than private collections. The authorities emphasised that any future salvage would require formal licensing, environmental impact assessments, and ongoing consultation with communities, scholars, and descendant groups. “Treasure hunting is not the point here,” said The Rt Hon. Mairéad Phelan, minister for Heritage in Northern Ireland. “What matters is the preservation of a cultural asset that tells us more about the era, the people, and the global trade networks that shaped the world. We will not permit the wreck to become a showpiece; it will be a resource for education and research that is accessible to the public.” Among those who watched the operation with a mix of caution and curiosity were local divers who have worked on the Girona site before. They spoke of a renewed respect for the wreck and its fragile state. One elder diver, who would not be named, recalled the first time he laid eyes on the site and the moment the water parted to reveal a glint of metal—an incident that changed his life and his sense of history. “Treasure is a surface thing,” he said. “The real treasure is the story—the way people moved across oceans, the way they traded, prayed, and fought. We have a duty to guard that story for future generations.” Scholars emphasise that the long-term value will come from systematic study rather than a single haul. The coins and metal fittings, for instance, can be subjected to metallurgical analysis to determine their provenance and the methods used to produce them. That, in turn, may help historians understand the broader supply chains that fed the Armada and the broader geopolitics of the late 16th and early 17th centuries. Some of the recovered objects bear marks of damage consistent with a violent encounter—likely the violent storm or the moment of wrecking when the Girona capsized or sank. The team cautions against drawing premature conclusions, noting that every artefact has a story, and many may have travelled beyond their original destinations before being buried in the seabed. Researchers say the site is actively monitored to prevent unauthorised disturbance. They stress that any further fieldwork will be undertaken only with proper permits and under the supervision of specialists in maritime archaeology and conservation science. The delicate balance between bringing the past to light and safeguarding it from the ravages of time remains a central challenge. In the months ahead, the team plans to complete the initial catalogue of artefacts, run condition assessments, and collaborate with international experts to develop a research programme that can be presented to the public. The eventual aim is not merely to display a manner of wealth but to present a narrative of exchange, risk, and human endeavour across oceans. The Girona’s wreck has long sparked debate about whether the Armada’s legacy should be celebrated, studied, or contained within museums. For many, the search today signals a new era for underwater archaeology—one in which technology, law, and local voices work in concert to illuminate a past that continues to cast a long shadow over the present. As the water settles over the site and the last of the afternoon light fades into the murk, the researchers gather their notes and prepare for the next phase. The treasure, they say, is a key not to a chest alone but to a corridor into which historians can walk—guided by the careful hands of scientists, the steady discipline of divers who know their duty, and the enduring curiosity of people who want to understand how a ship that sailed from Spain to the New World became a shared memory in a place as far away as Northern Ireland. What happens next is still being written, in the calm of the sea and the careful, measured language of museums and guardians of heritage. But for now, the Girona’s long voyage continues to yield its lessons, coin by coin, artifact by artifact, reminding us that the sea keeps its own, patient record of the past—and that sometimes the deepest discoveries are made not by those who chase fame, but by those who choose to protect what remains beneath the waves.

title: It's been a jam-packed year for the Get Inspired team.
text_ai: From the Rio Olympics and Paralympics, London Marathon and FA People's Cup to our fantastic campaigns Body Positive and Make Your Move, we've aimed to get the nation active by bringing you the most inspirational stories from members of the public with an extraordinary passion and dedication to sport. The team produced more than 60 feature films and explainer pieces, from day-by-day athlete diaries to quick-fire explainers that unpack the science of performance. The London Marathon and FA People’s Cup coverage were equally central to our mission: to show sport as a catalyst for connection. We streamed training runs, warm-up rituals, and the energy of mass-participation races, highlighting stories from first-timers to veterans who’d swapped fear for finish lines. For the People’s Cup, our team worked with grassroots clubs to capture the grit and creativity of amateur football—teams formed in schools, workplaces, and community halls, where a kickabout can become a doorway to confidence. Across these events, Get Inspired became a prism for communities to see their own potential reflected back in sport. Our campaigns stepped beyond the event calendar and into everyday life. Make Your Move has connected with communities in ways that feel practical and welcoming, inspiring people who’d previously felt shut out to take the first step—whether that’s a 5k rather than a sprint, or a gentle jog with a friend rather than a solo effort. The year also brought a gallery of extraordinary people who reminded us why these stories matter. There was the 16-year-old runner who found a sense of purpose after a health scare and discovered not just speed but a new circle of mentors; the wheelchair basketball player who balanced elite sport with higher education and advocacy; the retired teacher who used cycling to reconnect with neighbours and pupils alike. Beyond the joyful chaos of events and the long hours of shoots, the Get Inspired team has worked hard to build partnerships that amplify these voices. We’ve collaborated with national governing bodies, schools, health organisations, and local authorities to embed sport and activity into community life. The aim is sustainable change—new members in clubs, more inclusive PE classes, and real opportunities for people to stay active as they grow older or face barriers they hadn’t anticipated. The numbers underline a broader trend: audiences are not simply consuming stories; they’re acting on them. Our content strategy has driven a steady rise in engagement across platforms, with thousands of comments, shares, and person-to-person messages that prove a BBC storytelling project can move people to get moving. The Get Inspired channel has become a hub where people can find practical guidance, emotional support, and a sense that there is a space for them in sport. We’ll continue to pair frontline reporting with community-led content, ensuring people see themselves reflected in the questions, the training, and the triumphs we cover. title: On a farm so parched that it looks like a desert, Monica Amaraki reaches for an old brass tap only to find that no water flows from it.
text_ai: Here in Namibia in southern Africa, a drought is intensifying, the soil has been turned into dust and animals are scouring the baked land for something to eat. Monica's village, Omagongati, is in the far north of the country, a region notorious for extremes of weather, but she says that the dry spell hitting her now has been longer and more severe than normal. Monica’s lips are dry as the dust that coats the fields. She wipes her brow with the sleeve of her shirt and looks toward the parched horizon as if hoping the heat might reveal a hidden source. “We used to have a flow here, enough to wash the dishes and still leave a little for the animals,” she says. “Now there is nothing. Not a drop.” In Omagongati, a village that sits just inside the edge of the Namibian scrub, the river that once carried life through this landscape is nothing more than a cracked bed of clay. The few remaining cattle wander in search of shade and graze on scrub that offers little nourishment. Chickens skitter in the dust, pecking at scraps and anything that tastes like water. Women wash clothes in small, well-timed splashes when the wind lifts the dust long enough to reveal a glimmer of moisture in the basin’s bottom. The brass tap Monica reaches is a relic from better years, a stubborn holdover from a time when the village could count on a reliable communal supply. Now it is an ordinary object that reflects a stubborn truth: the supply has vanished. Across the north of the country, communities like Omagongati are tightening belts in ways that threaten the social fabric as much as the soil. Farmers, who have tilled the same plots for generations, speak of a season that refused to arrive, then disappeared abruptly. “We plant hoping for rain, and the rain never comes,” says 62-year-old elder Ulenga Ndeve, whose family keeps the village’s few goats. “We pray, we wait, and we cut back where we can. That is how we survive now.” The consequences ripple outward: school attendance falls as children are needed to help collect water; families borrow money to buy scarce fuel for long trips to distant boreholes; and the local market, once a hub of exchange, has become a place of anxious bargain hunting where maize meal and cooking oil are rationed with neighbours. The drought is not an isolated incident but part of a longer arc that scientists say is being intensified by climate change. Namibia has always borne harsh weather, but rainfall has become more irregular and unpredictable. In recent months, the region’s brief wet spells have offered little relief, and the dry spells have stretched longer than in living memory. Meteorologists warn that the current pattern could persist, with El Niño-like conditions during the coming dry season likely to push temperatures higher and reduce any modest chance of recovery. For farmers who rely on seasonal rains, the forecast offers little comfort. Aid workers and government officials acknowledge the scale of the challenge. Emergency food distributions have begun in pockets of the north, and the government has mobilised resources to truck water to towns and villages where boreholes have run dry. But the pace and reach of assistance are constrained by budgets, logistics, and the sheer breadth of need across rural Namibia. The World Food Programme has warned that without sustained relief and a longer-term plan, households could slip further into malnutrition and poverty. UNICEF has focused on child welfare, stressing that the impact of drought on schooling and health can endure long after the rains return. The local economy, such as it exists in Omagongati, is increasingly precarious. Livestock, once the backbone of rural life, are thinning out. In recent weeks, cattle prices have plunged as buyers fear the animals’ poor condition and the costs of feed—scarce, expensive, and often contaminated—eat into families’ livelihoods. Some households have begun selling off goats and sheep at prices well below what it costs to raise them, a loss that compounds generations of work. For farmers who have borrowed to sustain their herds, the losses can be crippling. Yet even in the harshest moments, there are signs of resilience. Women in the village have formed small cooperatives to share scarce resources, barter water, and swap notes on drought-tolerant crops. Some households are experimenting with drought-resistant varieties of millet and sorghum, seeds that can endure drier soils and heat. A few households have invested in simple, solar-powered pumps that pull water from shallow groundwater, a move that has cut some of the distance and danger of trekking to distant boreholes. Community nurseries have sprouted in empty yards, growing hardy trees and shrubs that can stabilise soil and offer shade and fodder in harsh years. Aid agencies emphasise that long-term adaptation must go beyond emergency relief. They argue for investment in water security—restoring and protecting the resilience of groundwater, improving rural infrastructure, and expanding access to affordable irrigation technologies that work with the climate rather than against it. They also urge regional and national leaders to commit to climate-resilient farming practices, diversified income opportunities, and social protection that can buffer families when crises strike. “Drought is not a one-season crisis; it’s a slow erosion of the things that keep communities alive,” says a senior official from a humanitarian NGO operating in the region. “We need to plan for the long horizon if we are to prevent this becoming a permanent fixture.” In Omagongati, Monica remains pragmatic. She has learned to ration water carefully, to patch and reuse what little they have, and to lean on neighbours in the hardest hours. Her youngest child, a girl of eight, asks when the creek will run again, and the mother can only answer with a quiet hope that tomorrow might bring a few more drops, a cooler breeze, a little shade to ease the day’s heat. Off camera, a health worker from a nearby clinic notes rising concerns about nutrition and waterborne illnesses as families drink contaminated, unsafe water in desperate times. She speaks with measured caution about the delicate balance between water scarcity and health risks, stressing the importance of clean-water know-how and basic hygiene, even when resources are dangerously scarce. The clinic has become a frontline in a broader struggle—how to keep people healthy when their water is not just scarce, but also a potential hazard. As the sun climbs higher, the village’s routine—such as it is—sifts toward the questions that will define the months to come: Will a wet season arrive in time to save crops? Will international aid and domestic programs keep pace with the needs? Can families like Monica’s hold their heads above the dust long enough for relief to reach them? For now, Monica stares at the old brass tap and imagines the life that used to spill from it. “We will endure,” she says, her voice steady but tired. “We have no choice.” The rain, when it comes—if it comes—will not simply fall on Omagongati; it will fall on a community that has learned to measure time by the rhythm of the drought, and to endure, until the day the earth finally remembers how to keep its promise.

title: Dame Helen Mirren has said it would be "wonderful" if it became more fashionable not to wear make-up.
text_ai: The actress recently appeared without heavy make-up alongside actresses including Nicole Kidman and Lupita Nyong'o for the 2017 Pirelli Calendar. title: On this week's Tech Tent - your weekly status update on the technology business - we have three stories reflecting our current anxieties about the nature of our digital world.

In private conversations with industry, there’s broad agreement that the risk to critical infrastructure is the most troubling part of a threat landscape that grows more complex by the month. Campaigns and outside groups are turning to botnets and automated engagement tools to push topics, inflate supposed momentum, and drown out opposing voices. text_ai: Manoj Ladwa, a London-based political strategist, is the founder of Indians for Labour, a platform for Indians in Britain to talk to Labour politicians and policy makers.
