title: As German Chancellor Angela Merkel is fond of repeating, the EU accounts for just 7% of the world's population and a quarter of its gross domestic product (GDP) but as much as half of its welfare spending.
text_ai: Her underlying message is that Europe spends too much on social policies and thus has no choice but to retrench. Austerity is one reason for cuts, but other threats to the sustainability of the welfare state are more fundamental. They include dealing with an ageing population and adapting to evolving societal expectations. But the trade-off is not merely about spending. It is also about the type of protection Europe wants to guarantee in a world of rapid change, where productivity must rise and workers’ careers stretch ever longer. In the short term, governments have instead found themselves juggling deficits with a growing list of aging obligations, while political mandarins warn that simply trimming entitlements will not solve the underlying pressures. Eurostat and national statistical offices highlight a stark demographic arc. By 2050, the number of people aged 65 and over in the EU is projected to reach almost one in four of the population, with the ratio of workers to retirees narrowing sharply in many member states. In Germany, long the anchor of the European social model, the labour force is ageing as if on schedule, even as the economy remains among the bloc’s most robust. In Italy and Greece, where pensions have historically consumed a larger share of GDP relative to output, the demographic squeeze is even more acute. And in eastern Europe, the effect is compounded by emigration of younger workers in search of opportunities elsewhere. A Commission briefing last year laid out the dilemma in stark terms: without reform, the pension system could become unsustainable even if growth returns to trend. With Europe already devoting roughly one-fifth of public spending to social protection, even modest shifts in retirement ages or benefit formulas can reverberate through budgets, tax purses and, ultimately, political support for the welfare state itself. The same document warned against assuming that higher spending automatically translates into better living standards, noting that efficiency—how well money is spent—matters just as much as the size of the purse. The words of policy-makers reflect the tension. In Paris and Madrid, governments have pushed through pension reform packages that gradually raise the minimum retirement age and curb generous early retirement provisions that crystallise deficits. In Berlin, ministers have framed reforms as a necessary adjustment, not a retreat, arguing that extending working lives, boosting productivity and diversifying funding for old age are the only viable routes to preserve universal protection without crippling future generations. Yet these steps are not universally popular. Campaigners for current pensioners warn that delays and reductions will erode social compact; younger voters argue that the burden of saving for old age should not fall entirely on their shoulders. Beyond pensions, health care and long-term care costs are ballooning, driven by medical advances, rising expectations, and the premium attached to timely access to services. Healthcare systems in several member states have been lauded for universal coverage and high standards, but they are also experiencing cost pressures as rates of chronic illness grow and the care workforce ages. Long-term care, once a relatively muted concern, has burst into view in policy debates as populations live longer and households change shape—many rely on informal care from family members that cannot be sustained indefinitely without public support. The response is not simply to spend more. Reform efforts are increasingly framed around three pillars: boosting labour force participation, especially among women and older workers; improving the productivity of health and care systems; and reforming the financing of welfare provisions so that they are both fair and affordable across generations. Some countries are pursuing more aggressive strategies to raise participation: subsidised childcare, flexible working arrangements, and the promotion of lifelong learning to keep skills aligned with job markets in an era of automation and digitisation. Europe’s answer to the funding squeeze has multiple lines. One involves public pensions, where higher retirement ages are argued to be a necessity, not a luxury. Another is a drive to diversify funding—through credible public-private partnerships, more robust occupational pension schemes, and, in some cases, targeted tax incentives that encourage personal saving for old age. And a growing debate concerns the early years of life: investment in early education and care, believed by some economists to yield high returns by improving long-run productivity and easing the transition into work. The changing social contract has political consequences. In a number of member states, voters have shown intolerance for tax increases and for perceived inequities in how the welfare state distributes resources. The rise of eurosceptic and nationalist movements in some regions reflects a broader discomfort with the costs—and benefits—of the European model. But in other countries, there is still broad political consensus that some form of universal coverage remains a civilizational achievement, even if its financing and delivery require reform. EU-level policymakers stress that reform does not mean retreat. The so-called European Pillar of Social Rights, rehoused in discussions of social investment and lifelong learning, is framed as a common standard rather than a prescriptive blueprint. It calls for equal opportunities, fair working conditions, and adequate social protection, with a particular emphasis on vulnerable groups and the transition to a greener economy. In that sense, the debate is as much about how Europe modernises its welfare state as it is about how much money it spends. Analysts caution that there is no one-size-fits-all solution. The contours of reform will depend on each country’s budgetary space, political climate, and economic structure. Some economies with strong growth prospects and prudent public finances may navigate pension and health reforms with less friction. Others, especially where the population is aging faster or where political consensus is harder to build, may face more difficult choices. For Merkel, and those who share her concern that Europe cannot continue to rely on the post-crisis model indefinitely, the challenge is to chart a path that preserves the unity of the European social model while recognising its limits. The question is not only how to spend more or less money, but how to spend it smarter—how to secure care for the elderly, keep health systems solvent, and still invest enough in education and innovation to sustain prosperity for future generations. As the Union grapples with these questions, the broader global backdrop looms large: other regions face their own aging trials, and the balance of competitiveness and solidarity remains a live, evolving conversation. The choices Europe makes in the coming years—on retirement ages, care reform, and the funding of social protection—will shape not only its welfare state, but the credibility of its political project as a whole.

title: Police in Taiwan have named a man who they think was responsible for injuring more than 20 people by setting off a pipe bomb on a busy train.
text_ai: The suspect, 55-year-old Lin Ying-chang, was seriously injured and is still unconscious. Police reportedly matched his fingerprints to one found on part of the exploded device, which was found near him on the commuter train. The blast happened on Thursday in Taiwan's capital, Taipei. The motives behind the blast remain unclear. Rescue crews worked through the night as investigators combed the carriage and surrounding rail corridor for clues about what happened and why. Officials said more than 20 people were treated for injuries, with several in a critical condition, and hospitals said they were prepared for any further influx if needed. Police have named Lin Ying-chang, 55, as the man they believe was connected to the attack. He was seriously injured and remains unconscious in hospital. Authorities said fingerprint analysis linked to a print on a component of the device found near him on the train, a finding they described as a crucial piece of the early investigation. Security cameras on board and at the stations are being reviewed for more footage that could show the moments leading up to the blast. Investigators have also searched nearby hospitals and other facilities for witnesses who may have seen someone leave the scene or carry a bag or package that could explain the attack. The transport authorities acknowledged disruption to services, with the line involved temporarily suspended while investigators worked at the site. Rail operators said some trains resumed later in the day with adjusted timetables, and service levels were expected to return to normal gradually as clearance and safety checks continued. Witnesses described a scene of chaos as the blast tore through the carriage during a busy period. Emergency crews were on the scene within minutes, and passengers were evacuated with assistance from station staff and police. At this stage, there has been no claim of responsibility, and officials say the motive behind the blast remains unclear. Police urged anyone with information to come forward and said the inquiry would proceed with due care and thoroughness as they collect more evidence. Lin Ying-chang’s current condition and the full background to his involvement will be a focus of continuing reporting as the investigation unfolds.

title: Lee Selby produced a superb performance to beat Russia's Evgeny Gradovich and claim the IBF featherweight title.
text_ai: The Welshman, 28, boxed beautifully at times and left the champion chasing shadows for sustained periods. A clash of heads opened a nasty cut over Gradovich's right eye in the seventh and the doctor called the fight off in the following round. Selby's precision and feet impressed throughout, and for long spells Gradovich simply could not lay a glove on him. The 28-year-old from Barry, Wales, had promised a bold, aggressive display and delivered it with aplomb, slipping jabs and straight lefts through Gradovich's guard and nailing the Mexican-born former champion with clean counters whenever the rickety pace of the rounds allowed. The opening exchanges were telling. Selby, slick and composed, used the first couple of rounds to establish his range, stepping in and out with trademark accuracy as Gradovich pressed closer and tried to rough him up on the inside. The crowd roared with every crisp right hand, and Selby’s movement made Gradovich's work rate look laboured by comparison. When Gradovich did land, it was usually a clubbing shot on the gloves, the Welshman deftly rolling with the shots and returning fire with a sharp left hand that found its mark more than once. Gradovich never lost his tenacity; the former world champion remained dangerous whenever he could pin Selby to the ropes. Yet Selby’s lateral movement, the way he kept his left hand high and his jab glued to Gradovich’s face, made the Russian-born challenger chase shadows for extended stretches. It was a performance that reinforced the sense that Selby had arrived at a level well beyond his previous battles. The turning point came in the seventh round, when a clash of heads opened a nasty cut over Gradovich’s right eye. Blood immediately began to trickle down the side of his face, staining the tape and the canvas in a stark red line. The ringside doctor moved in and, after examining the cut, waved Gradovich to continue. But as the eighth played out, the pain and the damage appeared to take a toll, and Gradovich’s movement slowed, his legs tiring as Selby increased the tempo with a sustained, almost clinical assault. Selby pressurised behind a stiff jab, then cracked Gradovich with a crisp right hand that snapped the champion's head back and drew a sharp exhale from the crowd. It was the sort of sequence that made it clear – to anyone who hadn’t already grasped it from the prior rounds – that the Welshman was the sharper, keener operator on the night. Gradovich’s corner threw in the towel of sorts, in the sense that they signalled to the doctor that their man could not defend himself with the necessary level of authority. The doctor walked to the center of the ring, and after a brief consultation with the referee, signalled that the fight could not continue. The official result confirmed Selby as the new IBF featherweight champion, a victory that came by way of a doctor stoppage early in the eighth round. It was a triumph built on an all-round, composed performance, not a one-punch finish, and it underlined a breakout moment for a fighter whose stock had been rising for years. Selby did not disguise his relief in the immediate aftermath. “This is what I’ve fought for my whole life,” he said, his voice steady but thick with emotion. “To win a world title in front of my own people means everything. I’ve dreamed of this moment since I was a boy, and to have it come true is something you can’t put into words.” Gradovich, still calm in defeat, offered praise for his conqueror and vowed to come again. “He was the better man tonight,” he said, acknowledging the need to reassess after this setback. “I’ll go back, train hard, and come back stronger. It’s part of boxing.” The atmosphere in the arena had been electric long before the final bell, and it reached fever pitch as Selby rose to receive the belt and clap hands with his team. The ring was a sea of congratulatory smiles, the crowd chanting the Welshman’s name and offering a sustained roar of approval as he lifted the IBF belt aloft. The match had been billed as a tactical test as much as a clash of champions, and Selby delivered on both counts. His feet were a constant asset, enabling him to slip in and out of range while keeping Gradovich from establishing any rhythmic rhythm that might have allowed him to impose his will. It was not a one-sided affair; Gradovich pressed with grit, but Selby never allowed the pressure to become a sustained problem, and when the moment came to end it, the finish was the inevitable extension of a performance built on discipline and speed. The win places Selby at the forefront of a busy featherweight division, with a number of possible routes opening up in the calendar. A unification fight would seem a logical route for a fighter who has consistently demonstrated the ability to adapt his approach to different styles. Promoters were already talking in terms of potential matchups with other champions and top contenders, while fans began speculating about where the new champion might plot his next move. For Gradovich, tonight is a setback of the harshest kind, but a veteran of the sport’s toughest moments. He walked back to the locker room with his resolve intact, and his team signified that, despite the defeat, there is life in him yet for another assault on a world title. In the immediate days ahead, Selby’s team will seek to frame the next steps, the terms of which will be shaped by the conversations with the sanctioning body and potential challengers who have long waited for a chance to test themselves against a man who has just shown he can wear a world title with the poise of a seasoned veteran. As the crowd began to filter out of the venue, the sense lingered that a new chapter had opened for Welsh boxing. Lee Selby, with a measured smile and a belt gleaming by his side, had earned more than a title tonight; he had reinforced his status as one of the sport’s most technically accomplished operators and given fans a glimpse of the longevity that can accompany a fighter who fights with such fluency and purpose.

title: Expectations of a rise in interest rates has prompted a pick-up in mortgage activity, and unsecured borrowing has also increased.
text_ai: Although timing of any rate rise is far from certain, the British Bankers' Association (BBA) said "competitive" deals had driven increased lending. Personal loan and credit card borrowing have also increased, the BBA said. The figures come as Citizens Advice warned that problem debt for young adults is on the increase. Lenders said the turnaround had been broad-based, spanning both fixed and variable-rate products. The BBA noted that mortgage approvals for home purchases had edged higher in the latest period as lenders continued to compete for borrowers with a mix of discounted and fixed-rate deals. Remortgaging also remained a feature, with homeowners seeking to lock in more favourable terms ahead of any rise in policy rates. The increase in unsecured lending followed suit, with personal loans and credit cards contributing the most to the uptick. Banks and building societies told the association that borrowers were using new credit to cover a range of expenses, including repayments on existing debt, home improvements and everyday costs as living expenses continued to bite for many households. Mortgage market activity has been helped, to some extent, by more generous lender incentives. A number of lenders have broadened eligibility criteria slightly and trimmed some initial rates in a bid to attract borrowers amid ongoing competition. Analysts cautioned that such deals can be attractive in the short term but may not reflect long-term affordability for all borrowers, especially if rates rise. Citizens Advice said the rising cost of living, coupled with higher debt levels among younger adults, was driving more people to seek help. The charity said debt-advice demand from under-25s had increased significantly in recent months, with many reporting juggling repayments to cover essentials or to manage rent and student loan payments. It called for clearer information on borrowing costs and more robust protections for vulnerable borrowers. Economists stressed that while the uptick in lending signals demand from households, it also underscored the sensitivity of consumer finances to any shift in interest-rate expectations. If rates rise, debt servicing costs could tighten budgets quickly for borrowers with near-limit credit facilities. Banks have noted that affordability checks remain strict, but lenders warned that rising living costs could push more households into stress if rates move higher. The Bank of England’s next moves, and the trajectory of rates in the coming months, will shape the tone of the housing and credit markets into the second half of the year. Market watchers say a cautious approach by lenders is likely to persist as they balance competitive offers with borrowers’ ability to cope if borrowing costs climb further.

title: The NHS has come under intense pressure this winter, with record numbers of patients facing long waits in accident and emergency units among other challenges.
text_ai: We asked some of those who have fallen ill, and the families of others, to share their experiences of winter 2016-17. My dad's mental health has really deteriorated - I blame the trauma of the fall and the time he's been forced to spend in hospital Sue's father's life changed dramatically after he fell out of bed while in hospital in December 2016. Across the country, families tell of nights spent waiting in a corridor, or of the ache of a loved one lying on a chair rather than in a bed. Some describe moments of quiet panic when a parent’s condition worsened while they waited for a doctor to become free, and others recall the relief when help finally arrived, only to be followed by a new period of uncertainty as care plans were drafted and revised. Jill, whose mother fractured her hip after a fall in late December, says the experience has left them physically exhausted and emotionally drained. “We ended up on a ward where the lights never went off and the noise never stopped,” she recalls. “There were three of us in a single room, and every nurse seemed rushed to the point of being invisible. My mum needed pain relief, and we felt we were pleading for something as simple as a swabbed wound to be checked.” In another family, David watched his father’s condition deteriorate after a fall on an icy path in early January. “We were told he would be moved to a bed that day, then the next day, then the next,” he says. “By the time a decision was made, several days had passed and the strain on him—physically and mentally—was clear.” He describes a sense of being trapped between urgent care and the slow pace of discharge planning, a problem that can compound the stress of lengthy hospital stays. For many patients, the concern wasn’t just the wait in A&E but the broader pattern of care. A nurse from a district general hospital in the north of England described a shift in focus from treating acute injuries to managing risk and throughput. “We’re trying to push people through safely and quickly, but the system feels like it’s built for the numbers we’re not allowed to ignore,” she says. “If a patient could be kept more effectively in a community setting, they would be, but there simply aren’t enough social care beds or home support to make that possible.” The pressures have been most visible at the nation’s busiest emergency departments, where long queues and crowded bays became routine narratives through December and January. Ambulance services faced delays in transferring patients from the vehicle to the hospital bed, and hospital leaders warned that every minute a patient waited to be admitted could worsen outcomes. In some trusts, directors spoke of “trolley waits” stretching into hours as a bed finally became available, while staff tried to preserve dignity and privacy in overcrowded spaces. Families living outside urban centres described the additional challenge of getting to hospital and back home again when public transport schedules did not align with the demands of visiting hours. In rural areas, with limited hospital capacity, the journey could be long and arduous, sometimes requiring an overnight stay in line with medical needs rather than personal preference. The NHS has repeatedly argued that the spring and summer of 2016 left hospitals juggling higher numbers of seriously ill patients than in previous winters, with a consequential carry-over into 2017. A spokesperson for NHS England pointed to a combination of factors: higher flu levels than expected, a larger elderly population with frailty and chronic illnesses, and delays in discharging patients into appropriate social care settings due to shortages outside hospitals. Behind the stark statistics lie human costs that colleagues describe as growing by the day. Dr Maria Patel, a consultant at a teaching hospital, emphasises the double bind facing clinicians: “We know what we need to do for each patient, but the system often prevents the speed at which we can do it. You can have gold-standard medical decisions, but if you can’t get a bed, or you can’t arrange the necessary social care when you leave, the best plan sits on a shelf.” The government and NHS leadership have highlighted steps taken in recent weeks to ease the winter pressure. A winter plan announced before the peak period aimed to increase capacity by boosting staffing levels, expanding the use of urgent care centres, and encouraging hospitals to work more closely with local authorities on discharge arrangements. The plan also included financial support to social care services and home care providers to help people return home more quickly when feasible and safe. Nevertheless, the impact of the pressures has been felt across broader services. Elective procedures—surgeries scheduled in advance rather than in emergencies—were among the first to be postponed when capacity became tight. In many hospitals, waits for hip and knee replacements, cataract surgery, and some cancer-related procedures stretched longer than usual. While NHS managers insist that clinical safety remains the priority, the knock-on effects were visible in clinics across the country as doctors and nurses reported backlogs building in outpatient settings. In the mental health arena, specialists warned that winter conditions—separated families, isolation, and stress from hospital stays—could aggravate existing conditions and complicate treatment for some patients. In several London trusts, psychiatrists reported a rise in emergency referrals as people faced barriers to regular therapy or medication management during the cold months. Social workers noted that the demand for community-based support rose in step with hospital discharges, placing added pressure on services that have been chronically underfunded. Data published during the period underscored a troubling pattern: a higher number of patients presenting at A&E departments and longer average waiting times, combined with a strain on ambulance handovers and bed occupancy rates near or at capacity. NHS England and academic health science centres argued that the winter surge was not simply about cold weather but about structural issues in the health and social care system that intersect in the channels between hospital and home. Public health experts pointed to flu as a significant driver of the increased demand. A severe flu season can quickly translate into more people requiring hospital care, particularly among older adults and those with chronic illnesses. One clinician noted that the combination of seasonal illnesses with a backlog of regular care created a “perfect storm” for crowded wards and stretched staff. The conversations around what can be done to break the cycle have intensified as winter turns to spring. Some experts argue that a more integrated approach to health and social care—one that aligns hospital discharge planning with robust community support—offers the best hope for reducing avoidable admissions and shortening waits. Others caution that without a sustained increase in funding and workforce, the system may continue to operate near its breaking point during the coldest months of the year. In this broader debate, patients and families have a clear message: any improvements must be felt on the ground, in wards and in consultation rooms, and not just in policy documents. They want to know that the NHS can deliver urgent care when it is needed, that waiting times will be monitored and managed, and that the emotional and logistical burdens placed on families will be acknowledged and addressed. Health ministers have urged the public to use urgent care facilities judiciously, emphasising that not every illness requires an emergency response and that choosing the right service can help relieve pressure at the busiest times. NHS England has also stressed the importance of safe and timely discharge, with social care partners asked to ensure that community and home-based support is available to those who no longer need hospital care but still require assistance. The winter of 2016-17 has prompted a wide-ranging national conversation about the resilience of the NHS and the social care system that supports it. It has highlighted both the boundless commitment of frontline staff and the limitations of a system stretched by demographic change and rising demand. For many families, the experience has sharpened a sense of vulnerability: the fear that a serious health event can trigger a cascade of complications that extends far beyond the initial illness. In the months following the height of the crisis, hospitals and local authorities began to publish more granular data on discharge times, bed occupancy, and the performance of urgent care pathways. Analysts and health service researchers have called for longer-term reforms to address the structural causes of winter pressure: investment in community health services, better integration between health and social care, and a workforce strategy that ensures experienced, stable staffing through peak periods. For those who faced it firsthand, the winter was not just a test of medical infrastructure but a test of the human capacity to care under strain. The stories people tell—of waiting, of fear, of relief when a bed finally became available—reflect the daily realities of a system that serves millions, day in and day out. They also serve as a reminder that health care is as much about relationships and communication as it is about diagnosis and treatment: the timeliness of a response, the clarity of information given to families, and the dignity afforded to patients in the most vulnerable moments. As the country moves forward, the challenge remains to convert the lessons of the winter into lasting change. The NHS is compelled to balance the immediate demands of crisis management with the longer-term goal of sustainable, high-quality care for all. In the weeks and months ahead, officials say, the focus will be on strengthening the ties between hospital services and community-based supports, investing in the workforce, and delivering improvements in discharge planning and out-of-hospital care. For now, the memories that linger for those who watched a loved one wait for care are the personal markers of what winter 2016-17 tested and, in many cases, revealed about the resilience of a health system that remains essential to the nation’s wellbeing. The questions that remain—about funding, staffing, social care capacity, and the pace of reform—will continue to shape the policy conversations that follow this challenging period. And for families still navigating the aftermath, every day serves as a reminder of the work still required to ensure that help comes quickly, compassionately, and safely when it is needed most.

title: The NHS should get a "Brexit bonus" of £5bn a year, former Conservative Health Secretary Andrew Lansley has said.
text_ai: Speaking at the NHS Providers annual lecture, Lord Lansley said the public had a right to expect extra funding, which should be in place by 2019-2020. He also called for ministers to commit to spending 7% of GDP on the NHS. Mr Lansley used the platform to press for a written guarantee from ministers, arguing that the NHS should be allowed to plan with a stable, longer‑term funding settlement. He suggested the extra cash could be targeted at core services, staffing and the capital programme, rather than short‑term quick fixes. The former health secretary also warned that without a credible plan for growth in public spending, the NHS would struggle to keep pace with rising demand, particularly for mental health and social care integration. He told the audience the government should not simply shuffle money around or make ad hoc changes, but deliver a firm commitment to a longer‑term funding trajectory. His remarks come amid ongoing debate inside Westminster about what kind of financial settlement the NHS will receive in the coming years, with ministers under pressure to articulate a clear plan for spending as Brexit unfolds. NHS Providers’ chief executive Chris Hopson welcomed the discussion, while urging caution. “Any increase in funding has to be matched with a credible plan for workforce, reform and capital investment,” he said. “The NHS remains under pressure from rising demand and real‑term restraints on staffing and beds.” Labour accused the former minister of using a headline figure to drive a political narrative. Jonathan Ashworth, the shadow health secretary, said the priority should be safeguarding and increasing funding through a stable, non‑Brexit dependent route. “The NHS needs a clear, funded plan, not slogans about a Brexit windfall,” he said. A government spokesperson said no decision had been taken on the scale or the source of any post‑Brexit funding for the NHS and urged stakeholders to avoid “pretend windfalls,” stressing that any changes would be set out in due course within the context of the overall public finances.

title: Falling global demand for personal computers (PC) saw shipments fall by a record 10.6% in the fourth quarter from a year ago, according to market research firm IDC.
text_ai: About 71.9 million units were shipped in the period, which includes the key Christmas shopping season. IDC said the decline was the worst since it started tracking PC shipments. PC demand has been hit by competition from smartphones and tablets, along with longer lifecycles for PCs. The IDC figures add to a growing picture of a market that has now entered a more prolonged period of contraction. The research group said demand was weakest in consumer segments, where buyers have become more selective amid higher borrowing costs and inflation, while business buyers continued to pace their refresh cycles more slowly than in previous years. Regionally, Asia-Pacific bore the sharpest decline in the quarter, IDC said, with shipments falling at double-digit rates in several major markets. Western Europe and North America also posted declines, though the rate of fall was more modest in the latter, where many buyers had switched to mid-range laptops already in the pipeline. Latin America and the Middle East were described as mixed, with some pockets of demand in education and government work offsetting softness in other sectors. The weaker quarterly performance comes after a year in which PC shipments had already been under pressure from a shift in consumer appetite away from devices with smaller screens toward more multifunctional tablets and smartphones. Longer replacement cycles, driven by higher prices and the practical utility of current devices, have left many shoppers delaying purchases until late 2024 or beyond, IDC noted. Analysts said the fourth-quarter lull reflected a combination of factors rather than a single driver. In addition to price sensitivity, supply constraints that lingered earlier in the pandemic era have largely eased, allowing manufacturers to operate more efficiently, but that has not translated into a surge of demand. The result is a market that is whether and when to replace an existing PC remains a key question for households and corporate buyers alike. For manufacturers, the immediate response has been to recalibrate inventories and focus on segments with stronger pull, such as business laptops, education devices and, in some cases, premium gaming notebooks. Price competition has intensified as vendors seek to protect share in a market where the mix of cheap consumer models and higher-end machines is shifting. IDC’s assessment is that the PC market is unlikely to return to the growth rates seen during the early pandemic years in the near term. Still, the firm cautioned that demand could stabilise in late 2024 if consumer confidence improves and supply chains stay orderly, with any rebound likely to be gradual rather than swift. Industry executives will be watching closely for signs of demand reviving in the first half of next year, along with early indicators from enterprise buyers who may begin to refresh once budgets are approved for the next fiscal cycle. title: Far more men than women are dying from skin cancer, despite similar numbers being diagnosed with the disease, a report suggests.

title: Little by little, plans are leaking out regarding the imminent battle to remove so-called Islamic State (IS) from Mosul, Iraq's second largest city.
text_ai: Michael Fallon, the UK defence secretary, said military co-operation agreements were finalised on 23 September, adding that "the encirclement operation will begin in the next few weeks" with Mosul being liberated "in the next few months". Behind the closed doors of a string of recent military briefings, a three-pronged plan for Mosul has begun to emerge from the fog of speculation that has surrounded the battle for Iraq’s second city. Western and Iraqi officials say the idea is to seal off Mosul from all sides, then press a carefully staged assault on the urban heart of the ISIS caliphate stronghold. Officials stress the timetable has always been contingent on the on‑the‑ground reality in Mosul, not on rhetoric. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s public commitment to an Oct. 19 start date for the operation has added a new dimension to an already complex coalition dynamic, with Ankara signalling it would play a robust role in the campaign’s initial phase. From the air, coalition jets have been pounding ISIS supply lines and command posts in and around Mosul, while refuelling and logistics hubs in northern Iraq have been expanded to support a longer campaign. The United Nations and aid groups have warned that even with concerted precautions, the assault risks forcing hundreds of thousands of civilians to flee their homes. In the last weeks, aid agencies have been racing to pre‑position relief stocks, establish corridors for civilians seeking to leave, and increase medical capacity in camps across northern Iraq. UN figures suggest the population of Mosul and surrounding districts is in the region of 1.5 million people, with a significant proportion thought to still be inside the city. The potential for bottlenecks—blocked roads, collapsed bridges and the city’s fractured electricity and water networks—could compound the risk to civilians. The World Food Programme has prepared additional food distributions, and the International Committee of the Red Cross has been negotiating access to besieged districts for urgent medical care and the safe return of trapped residents. They stress the importance of credible corridors and verified civilian transfers, as well as the need for safeguarding medical facilities and schools in areas not controlled by ISIS. Yet the city’s 2014 seizure by ISIS, followed by years of insurgency and counter‑insurgency, left behind a fragile social fabric and a multiplicity of local loyalties that could complicate post‑battle governance. In its prime, a Top of the Pops appearance could elevate a track from obscurity to export status, and a single week’s guest list could double as a cultural snapshot: a chorus of haircuts, fashions, and ever-shifting attitudes all on one stage and one screen. The early decades are best remembered for a sense of discovery. The show’s opening titles—a swinging, chart-topping cascade of graphics and a soundtrack that promised a new week of possibilities—introduced viewers to acts who would go on to become global icons. The camera’s eye moved quickly, almost as if to keep pace with the music, panning between the studio’s stage and its surrounding audience, or cutting back to a rotating display of the week’s hottest videos. Performances, when they occurred, were as much about the moment as the melody: a fresh, sometimes startling doorway into a hit that might otherwise have traversed radio alone. In an era with few visual archives of a chart-topping single, Top of the Pops gave viewers something they could not easily obtain elsewhere—a shared, televised event that bound families, friends, and the nation in a single televised night. As the years rolled on, the show’s fabric was repeatedly rewoven to reflect shifts in the music industry. The 1970s brought a glitter and a grind—glam rock, disco’s electric pulse, and a fashion language that would later be celebrated, or parodied, in countless retrospectives. The industrial light of the studio grew more sophisticated, and the programme’s set became a theatre in which trends could be tested, adjusted, or sublimated into a signature look. It was during these years that the show began to function not merely as a countdown but as a live portal to the chart’s social imagination: the audience’s reaction, the host’s banter, the occasional on-stage collaboration that felt almost mythic in the moment. The 1980s, meanwhile, helped push the programme from a national curiosity into a global cultural phenomenon. MTV had redefined the relationship between music and image, and Top of the Pops, with its brick-red sofa of hosts and a rotating cast of musicians appearing both solo and with live bands, offered a British counterpoint—an invitation to see the music you heard on the radio mirrored in a visual language of fashion, choreography, and performance. The show’s dance segments—carefully choreographed to be both entertaining and accessible—became part of the show’s identity. It was not merely about the single; it was about the whole moment: the outfits, the hair, the stage lighting, the stagecraft, the sense that you were witnessing a piece of popular culture being curated in real time. The 1990s brought another transformation, one that reflected a global shift in how music was consumed. The advent of wider cable coverage and the rise of the internet began to erode the primacy of a weekly countdown as a primary means of discovery. Yet Top of the Pops retained a singular ability to repackage a song’s appeal for television. Acts who would not yet be household names found themselves launched into households through the programme’s familiar rhythm: the countdown’s momentum, the televised performance, the host’s concluding remarks that could tip the balance of perception from merely hearing a track to feeling its potential significance. The Spice Girls’ first big wave, Britpop’s raucous revival, and the late-90s wave of pop exports found a stage in TOTP’s studio that could make a city’s worth of music fans feel temporarily connected to something larger than their local charts. In the new millennium, the programme encountered fresh pressures. Digital platforms, streaming services, and social media changed how fans connected with music. A song could find an audience with fewer gatekeepers, and audiences—once a predictable, live studio audience with a strong sense of ritual—began to fragment into micro-communities who consumed content in a more on-demand fashion. The BBC, which had once defined national listening habits, found itself competing with a constellation of platforms for attention. The format—a studio-based, live-feeling performance with a host guiding viewers through the week’s top tracks—could feel quaint or outdated, depending on the observer and the moment. The decision to discontinue the programme was not framed as a death but as a reevaluation of how the BBC should discharge its responsibilities to music culture in a changing media environment. The Corporation argued that the weekly, mass-audience model no longer aligned with how people actually engage with music in 2013. International streaming platforms offered intimate access to the very acts that the show had once hyped to national audiences. YouTube had already turned the world into a vast, searchable archive: fans could watch a single performance again and again, whenever they wished, instead of waiting a week for the next instalment. The value of the ongoing “Top of the Pops moment” was measured not in the curation of a weekly chart but in the living, breathing, moment-to-moment experience of music across multiple channels and devices. There were, of course, those who mourned the decision as a symbolic end of a certain form of shared culture. A generation of viewers who had grown up with the show—parents who had introduced their children to new acts on a quiet Thursday edition, or teenagers who had learned how to “dance like everybody else” to a particular beat—felt a personal sense of loss. For them, the programme had been not merely a source of entertainment but an anchor in a world that often felt bewildering. The show’s removal did not erase its memory; rather, it reframed it as a nostalgic artifact with a continuing, if intermittent, afterlife in retrospectives, documentaries, and special editions. It is a sign of Top of the Pops’ stubborn cultural gravity that, even as its weekly presence faded, the brand continued to surface in the public imagination. BBC4’s documentaries, the occasional one-off specials, and the revived interest in the programme’s history treated TOTP as a lens through which to examine Britain’s popular culture over half a century. A generation of music historians, pop journalists, and curators argued that the show had performed a distinct social function: not merely to chronicle, but to interpret, reflect, and sometimes even accelerate the mood of the moment. In that sense, its influence persisted even as the programme itself receded from the weekly schedule. To understand the decline, one must also consider the economics of television and the changing nature of the BBC’s commitments. A studio-heavy format with high production values, live performances, and a weekly cycle of guests required significant resources. The BBC pointed to cost, audience trends, and the availability of acts in an increasingly crowded media landscape as factors that made the weekly edition less viable. In addition, the BBC’s own strategy around “event” programming—where significant moments are captured in special editions—began to shift how it used its resources. An annual Christmas edition, when the nation tuned in with family and friends, could still perform a ceremonial function, but it needed to compete with other flagship programming to justify the attention and the license fee investment. Yet the programme’s absence did not go entirely unmarked. The BBC has from time to time entertained the possibility of reviving TOTP in a form that might fit the modern media ecosystem—one that could draw on streaming, social media, and the ability to tailor a show for a global audience. The idea of a revamp is not a rejection of the brand but an acknowledgment of a changing appetite: audiences crave access, immediacy, and interactivity in ways a traditional studio-based format has found challenging to provide. The BBC, in public statements, has stressed that while Top of the Pops remains a vital part of its heritage, any revival would need to be built around contemporary listening habits and new technology rather than a direct rehash of the old format. There is another dimension to this story, one that speaks to the programme’s place in Britain’s musical memory. The show acted as a kind of public archive of styles, moments, and performances. A viewer who recalls a particular guitar riff from an early-70s record might also remember the lighting cues and the host’s quip that made the moment feel as if it belonged to them as much as to the artist on screen. For many, it is the memory of those tiny, almost incidental details—the clack of the studio microphone, the way the dancers’ silhouettes moved under the spinning lights—that preserves a tangible link to a period when television and pop music were still learning how to coexist in a shared national space. That cultural residue is, in many ways, its lasting legacy. The show helped democratise pop culture in a way few programmes could: it put a spotlight on acts who had yet to break through, it gave viewers a portal into an industry that could feel distant, and it allowed for a weekly conversation about what music meant in a country of many languages, classes, and influences. The ability to watch a chart in motion—the rise of a single from number 40 to number 1, the drama of a new entry, the surprise appearance of a then-unknown artist who would go on to redefine a genre—was a shared, nation-sized event. For that reason, even now, people often reference a specific edition as a touchstone: a particular performance, a memorable joke, a fashion moment that defined a decade. Today, as the industry continues to reinvent itself, the BBC’s stance on Top of the Pops is both reverent and practical. The corporation recognises that while the programme cannot simply be revived as it was, there is value in its name and what it represents. In an era when a single video can travel the world in seconds and a chart is as likely to be a playlist as a list of numbers, the “Top of the Pops” concept—celebrating the act of making music public—still has resonance. The challenge lies in translating that resonance into a form that can sustain audiences across multiple platforms and a global audience accustomed to instant access. In the meantime, the show’s absence invites another kind of conversation: what, precisely, is the role of a national broadcaster in a music ecosystem that has become far more diverse and decentralised than it was half a century ago? Is there space for a flagship music programme that is curated for the public good rather than for sponsorship or share of viewing? And, perhaps most pertinently for a nation that takes pride in its cultural output, can a programme with the reach of Top of the Pops still define a moment in time for generations who will discover it not on a living room television, but on a screen that is ever present in their hands? Public discussion around these questions has not produced a simple answer. Some argue that the spirit of Top of the Pops lives on in smaller, more nimble formats: live music nights in community venues, national anniversaries of well-loved records, or short-form video series produced specifically for online audiences. Others contend that the BBC’s reluctance to revive the weekly format is a sign of respect for the audience’s evolved expectations rather than a surrender to the convenience of streaming. In either view, the BBC’s decision has allowed for a broader set of possibilities—to celebrate pop music in fresh ways, while preserving the memory of a programme that once defined the national conversation about what was popular. There is, of course, a broader context to this story. The history of Top of the Pops can be read as a mirror to the history of British popular culture—its anxieties, ambitions, and at times its contradictions. Its story intersects with fashion trends, with the dawning of the music video era, with the rise and fall of genres, and with the cyclical nature of fame itself. The show captured a country’s mood and, in doing so, often helped shape it. The measure of its influence is not merely in the numbers of people who watched it, but in the ways in which it became a shared cultural vocabulary—a shorthand through which many people could talk about a new song, a new artist, a new moment in time. Recent years have produced a renewed sense of nostalgia for the programme, especially among those who remember the early, more chaotic years when the studio could feel like a launchpad for a new generation of performers. In interviews and retrospectives, participants—presenters, dancers, sound engineers, and artists who performed on the show—have recalled the sense of privilege and pressure that came with appearing on Top of the Pops. The show’s set was a theatre built to showcase not only the music but the music’s potential to resonate with a mass audience. The cameras moved with a confidence that suggested music could be navigated by television as carefully as by the performers. For younger audiences, the memory of Top of the Pops persists through clips on social media, through snippets in documentaries, and through the occasional reissued compilation that collects the programme’s most enduring performances. The show’s legacy lives not only in the acts it spotlighted but in the idea that a weekly televised event could be a unifying cultural moment—a shared experience in an age of fragmentation. The debate about its future, then, is not just about nostalgia; it is about the potential for a new form of public music-making that respects the past while harnessing the tools the present affords. Of course, the people who watched Top of the Pops live are now adults with children of their own. Some will have introduced their own teenagers to the idea of a chart and a studio performance that was both serious and playful, a ritual that mixed ambition with a certain irreverence. In conversations with music fans, retailers, and cultural commentators, a recurring theme emerges: Top of the Pops was never merely about the songs on the list; it was about the social ritual surrounding those songs—the way communities formed around new pop moments, the way fashion and music coalesced in a space that felt both public and intimate at once. As the BBC contemplates its next steps in the field of music broadcasting, it remains to be seen whether a future “Top of the Pops” will ever truly fill the same role or whether a new flagship programme will supplant it as the nation’s weekly touchstone. What seems certain is that Top of the Pops, for all its years of transmission, continues to cast a long shadow. Its story has become part of the fabric of British popular culture, a reference point that continues to surface in discussions about how music and television intersect. In the end, the programme’s true value may lie not in a single episode or even in a single era, but in a willingness to imagine a moment when television could be the stage on which a country’s music was celebrated together, even if only for a half-hour a week. If a revival ever comes, it would likely do so not as a direct replication but as a reinvented companion—one that acknowledges the old show’s genius for spotlighting a hit while using contemporary technology to bring new energy to the same core idea: that music, when shared, becomes a more powerful thing. And so the end of TOTP’s weekly run does not mark the end of its influence. It marks a pause in a living conversation about how to present pop music to a nation—one that continues to reckon with the global, digital, always-on world in which we now live. The story of Top of the Pops is, in a sense, the story of British popular culture itself: a narrative of reinvention, of the tension between tradition and innovation, and, most of all, of a public that insisted on having a front-row seat to the music that sounded the times.

title: St Helens scored four of their five tries after the break as they came from behind to win at Castleford.
text_ai: The 2014 Super League champions were twice behind before finally seeing off depleted Castleford at the Jungle. Second row Joe Greenwood scored two of their tries, while Jonny Lomax followed up his two tries on his comeback against Leeds with Saints' final try. Castleford, fielding a patched-up backline and short of a couple of influential bodies, started on the front foot and looked to have the ascendancy as the second period began. Yet as the rain-soaked Jungle grew hushed, Saints found a way back into it, their pack laying the platform for another late-season salvage operation. Greenwood struck twice in quick succession, pouncing on loose ball near the Castleford line after a devastating Saints' spell. The second, a close-range finish after a sustained bit of pressure, put the onus on Cas to respond, which they did not without a fight. The Tigers, who had produced several spirited defensive stands, were unable to muster a clear counter-punch and began to run out of legs as Saints tightened the screws. An incisive move from the left set up the next Saints try, a crisp cross-field pass picking out Tom Makinson on the touchline. He carved infield and gave Saints a simple finish, the conversion of momentum turning the game in their favour. The Jungle sensed a shift, and the pendulum had clearly swung away from the hosts. Castleford’s day grew increasingly error-strewn as their discipline wavered under the Saints’ onslaught. Saints’ pressure told again when Lomax, returning to action with a goal to prove after his brace against Leeds, gathered a long ball on the right and twisted to touch down for Saints’ fourth. The move had started with a break from their No.9 and a bustling carry through the middle, culminating in Lomax’s clinical finish under the posts. By now the visitors had the upper hand and even a resilient Cas outfit looked a little disillusioned. Saints’ defence remained stubborn, repelling late Castleford forays and denying easily the quick strikes that could have rejuvenated a Tigers revival. The home side, with a threadbare squad and an injury list that would have unsettled a fuller-strength outfit, battled to keep the scoreboard respectable, but the scoreboard did not lie. When the whistle finally arrived, Saints had completed a remarkable turnaround from their first-half deficit to claim the win, four tries to one in the second half underscoring the visitors’ resilience. The result left Castleford with plenty to ponder as they headed back to their base, while St Helens, who had weathered the storm and found a different gear after the break, march on with renewed confidence. Castleford, for whom the absence of several key men was keenly felt, praised their spirit but conceded that Saints’ finishing power proved decisive. Saints, meanwhile, will take heart from a performance that suggested they can shrug off adversity and still grind out the results when it matters.

title: Babies who cry excessively and have problems feeding and sleeping have a greater risk of serious behavioural problems later in life, say scientists.
text_ai: One in five babies has symptoms that could lead to conditions such as ADHD, according to research published in Archives of Disease in Childhood. The review of previous studies looked at nearly 17,000 children. A child-health expert said it would be wrong for parents to be "overly alarmed" by the results. The researchers, who reviewed dozens of studies, emphasised that the associations observed do not mean that every baby with early crying or sleep and feeding problems will develop behavioural difficulties. They say that many children with such early symptoms go on to lead normal lives. The review drew on data from roughly 17,000 children across several cohorts and used a range of measures to capture behavioural outcomes in later childhood, including attention, activity and conduct. It found that groups with persistent infant distress tended to show higher rates of later problems, though the size of the risk varied between studies and was often modest. Experts cautioned that the findings should not prompt panic. “It would be wrong for parents to be overly alarmed by these results,” said Dr Rebecca Hale, a child-health physician not involved in the work. “What this shows is a pattern, not a prediction.” The authors also stressed that the causes of ADHD and related conditions are complex and multifactorial. They pointed to a combination of biological predispositions, parenting stress, and broader social factors that can influence a child’s development over years. In other words, early distress may be one of several contributors to later outcomes, rather than a single cause. Several clinicians urged families to seek support if infancy is difficult. Health professionals can offer guidance on sleep routines, feeding strategies and access to mental-health services for families under strain. “Early help can make a difference,” one paediatrician said, noting that supportive interventions for families can ease later problems even when the child has a predisposition to behavioural difficulties. The study’s authors called for more robust, long-term research to determine whether targeted early interventions could reduce the risk of later problems. They also urged health systems to ensure families have access to ongoing support as children grow, to better understand how early-life experiences shape later behaviour.

title: MPs' salaries will rise from £67,060 to £74,000, the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority has announced.
text_ai: The 10% pay rise has been approved despite Downing Street and a succession of MPs saying it was "not appropriate". IPSA chairman Sir Ian Kennedy said that MPs' pay had been a "toxic" issue "which had been ducked for decades". IPSA said the recommendation was the product of an annual independent review intended to reflect MPs’ duties, responsibilities and the level of work involved in representing constituents. It stressed the rise was not a response to political popularity but to a “twin imperative” of credibility and recruitment in a job with significant time demands and public scrutiny. Sir Ian Kennedy, the watchdog’s chairman, insisted the decision was taken in the wider context of the Parliament’s performance and standing. “This is not a prize for political service,” he said. “It is a recognition that the job of an MP has evolved, and that we must pay a rate that attracts capable people, while at the same time maintaining the public’s confidence in the institutions they elect.” He added that MPs’ pay had long been treated as a political football and warned that retreating from the issue would only deepen cynicism about Westminster. IPSA’s publicly stated aim is to balance fairness to MPs with public accountability. It said the review considered parliamentary workload, the demands of the role, and comparisons with other senior public sector roles. It noted that MPs face lengthy hours, frequent travel, and the obligation to represent a diverse and often contentious electorate. The body argued that a higher base salary would reduce the reliance on additional incomes from outside earnings for many MPs, which it said could improve transparency around the finances of flagship parliamentarians. The increase to £74,000 roughly translates to an annual rise of about £6,940 for each MP, before any adjustments for taxes, pensions, or other statutory deductions. When multiplied across the 650-odd MPs, the measure is estimated to add several million pounds to the annual cost of running Parliament. IPSA cautioned that the total cost of MPs’ remuneration, including non-salary allowances and staff costs, would rise accordingly, though it stressed that the pay award on its own is the central element of the decision. Downing Street responded with a cautious note. A spokesperson acknowledged the concerns voiced by many MPs and members of the public about the timing of any pay rise amid a cost-of-living squeeze. Yet the government emphasised that IPSA operates independently of ministers and Parliament, and that the rise would be implemented unless the independent body decided otherwise. The spokesperson reiterated that the government would not block the decision, while stressing that the optics of a pay rise in a difficult year were not lost on ministers. Opposition parties seized on the announcement as a reminder of Westminster’s disconnect from ordinary voters. A Labour spokesperson said the timing was “ill-judged” and suggested MPs should look to cutting the costs of Parliament or finding savings elsewhere before accepting a pay rise. The Liberal Democrats called for a broader package of reforms around MPs’ pay and expenses, arguing that trust in the system would only be restored if Parliament showed it could be more disciplined about high-fare salaries and the use of public funds. Taxpayers’ groups pressed for a more fundamental debate about why MPs need a high base salary at a time when public services face pressure. They warned that even a carefully calculated increase could feed into a narrative that Westminster is insulated from the realities faced by ordinary people. Some campaigners argued that any pay rise should be accompanied by stronger commitments to transparency, such as clearer disclosure of outside earnings and a tighter regime on expenses. The pay rise arrives amid days of controversy over the role and governance of Parliament. Critics have pointed to a perception of a “trust deficit” between MPs and the people they represent, arguing that pay policy should be tied more closely to performance, public results, and demonstrable reform. Proponents counter that MPs deserve a fair wage to perform demanding duties, particularly as the proportion of time spent on constituency work, committees, and scrutiny has grown. IPSA said it would publish a detailed breakdown of the new pay structure later this week, including how the base rate interacts with the various allowances that make up MPs’ total remuneration. It added that MPs’ pay would continue to be reviewed annually, with any changes arising from the next independent assessment determined by the same independent process. In a closing reminder of its remit, IPSA emphasised that the aim of the pay framework was not simply to compensate for time spent in Westminster but to recognise the responsibilities of representing diverse communities across the country, the pressures of decision-making in challenging times, and the long hours that the job can demand. As the country watches, MPs prepare to adjust budgets, and watchdogs monitor how the system is perceived; for many, the question remains whether the pay rise will help stabilise Westminster’s reputation or merely fuel another round of parliamentary debate about money.

title: US rapper Kanye West has been taken to hospital following an emergency services call, media reports say.

The Los Angeles Police Department said they were dispatched to the scene after a report of a disturbance but declined to identify the person involved. A spokesperson told the BBC the incident was later classified as a medical matter and that fire personnel were also sent to the location. The Los Angeles Fire Department confirmed an unnamed man had been taken to hospital for further assessment, but offered no further details about his condition. In a subsequent briefing, a police representative said the inquiry was in its early stages and that officers would not release additional information until family members or representatives had been notified. He added that investigations of this nature were standard practice and that information would be provided as soon as it became available. title: MSPs have started to put themselves forward in the contest to become Holyrood's next presiding officer.
text_ai: Labour's Ken Macintosh and Johann Lamont have announced their candidacy for the non-party role, while colleague Elaine Smith is considering a run. Conservative John Scott has put himself forward, while Murdo Fraser is considering joining the field. MSPs will elect an officer to replace Tricia Marwick at the first session of the new parliament on Thursday. The contest is being watched for signals about how Holyrood’s chamber intends to govern itself in the new session, with candidates stressing the need for steadiness and accessibility in debate. The Presiding Officer is responsible for enforcing the chamber’s rules, guiding procedure and chairing questions, while acting as a figurehead for Parliament in its relations with the executive and the public. In practice, the post requires calm cross‑bench leadership and a commitment to neutrality that lasts for the full term. Among those who have put their name forward, Ken Macintosh has emphasised a background in parliamentary procedure and a track record of maintaining order in debates. He has argued that the office should be used to improve backbench engagement, noting the importance of ensuring MPs from all sides have a genuine voice in proceedings. Johann Lamont, likewise, has highlighted the role of the Presiding Officer in safeguarding minority voices and ensuring that parliamentary scrutiny remains robust, particularly over time‑critical issues. Elaine Smith, the Labour colleague weighing up a bid, is expected to frame her approach around openness to constitutional and procedural reform, while stressing the need to keep Parliament accessible to the public. The Conservatives, with John Scott and Murdo Fraser both in the frame, have suggested that a seat at the table for skilled, pragmatic mediators could help to depoliticise the chair while continuing to respect party concerns outside the chamber. Party lines are not supposed to bind the winner, and MSPs will vote in a secret ballot to determine who takes on the role from the first session on Thursday. The short turn‑around between nominations and election means the field could narrow quickly, with backbenchers and committee chairs weighing the impact of a candidate’s previous parliamentary relationships on their ability to lead proceedings in a non‑partisan manner. Observers say the race will be about more than individual resumes. The new Presiding Officer will inherit a Parliament facing a crowded legislative agenda and ongoing questions about how best to balance rapid scrutiny with orderly debate. In that context, a candidate’s record on conciliation, time management and the ability to stand back from party politics could prove decisive. Cross‑party support is likely to be a critical factor. Even if a single candidate emerges with broad backing, the process routinely rewards a broad consensus figure who can command respect across the chamber. The current parliament has stressed the importance of collegiality in its running of business, and the outcome of Thursday’s vote will be watched as a bellwether for how easily the chamber can work together in the term ahead. Tricia Marwick’s successor will be expected to provide stability as Holyrood adjusts to the demands of a fresh mandate, a task that will require navigating sensitive votes, procedural quirks and the evolving relationship between Parliament and the Government. As the nominations crystallise and MSPs prepare to cast their ballots, the focus will be on who can best uphold the institution’s reputation for fair play and impartial leadership.
