title: Five of the six families promised an investigation following the deaths of their babies have been excluded from the official review.
text_ai: In November, the health secretary ordered a review of the "unnecessary" deaths of six babies at Crosshouse hospital in Ayrshire since 2008. But the BBC has learned it will only look at cases that have happened since December 2013. The review is being carried out by Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS). The decision to narrow the scope has prompted a chorus of concern from the families involved and from clinicians who say wider lessons could be learned only if every case is examined alongside system design and staffing levels at the time. The review, which was announced in November by the health secretary, is intended to examine the care provided in the Crosshouse hospital’s neonatal unit and to identify what went wrong in the six cases that resulted in the deaths of babies since 2008. But officials say the work will now focus on cases that occurred from December 2013 onwards, arguing that sufficient clinical records exist to support a thorough assessment and that extending the review further back would require resources beyond what has been allocated. A spokesman for Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) said the organisation would assess whether care met national standards, whether clinicians followed the relevant guidelines and whether the unit had appropriate oversight, governance structures and escalation processes. He emphasised that the review would not be a general audit of all neonatal care in Ayrshire, but a targeted look at the six deaths that prompted the inquiry and the care pathways leading to those outcomes. Yet for families who had believed the investigation would be comprehensive, the narrowing of the timeline has felt like a second wound. One parent, who asked to remain anonymous, described the decision as “shattering” and said it would leave important questions unresolved. “We want answers about what happened to our baby, and we want those answers to come from a process that doesn’t cherry-pick what it examines,” the parent said. In a briefing to parliament last month, the health secretary said the aim of the review was to learn lessons and to prevent similar tragedies in the future. He insisted the scope was deliberate, designed to deliver timely, concrete recommendations within a realistic framework. “Our priority must be patient safety and real, demonstrable improvements in care,” he said at the time. But critics say the narrow window risks producing a report that misses wider systemic issues that could have contributed to the fatalities, including staffing levels in the unit, access to specialist services, and the culture around escalation of concerns when a baby’s condition deteriorates. They argue that if the six deaths are not viewed within the full context of how care was organised in the years leading up to them, key factors may be overlooked. A spokesperson for the Scottish Conservatives described the decision as unacceptable to families who believed a full, independent review would be conducted. “If this is all we have, it will leave people asking why records from earlier years aren’t considered when the core issue is the quality and safety of care delivered in the neonatal unit,” they said. The health service’s own watchdog has faced questions about how it balances the need for timely, rigorous findings with the practicalities of retrieving and reviewing records that span more than a decade. HIS has indicated that even within the newer period, the review will rely heavily on the information contained in hospital records, incident reports, and statements from clinical staff. Where records are incomplete or missing, the organisation said, it would note those gaps and make recommendations aimed at improving record-keeping, governance, and patient safety culture. For families who had hoped for a broader inquiry, there is particular concern about where accountability sits in the process. They fear that limiting the scope to a recent period could obscure a pattern that extended beyond a single cohort or a particular time frame. In neonatal care, advocacy groups note, little changes unless there is a clear line-of-sight to long-term organisational learning. They emphasise that the most meaningful reforms frequently emerge when investigations consider the climate in which care was provided—staffing pressures, training deficits, and the systems used to monitor babies at risk of deterioration. The health secretary’s office said that while the review will not consider all six original cases in full, it would still address the core questions raised by families: whether there were delays in recognizing deterioration, whether appropriate escalation protocols were followed, and whether there were gaps in the use of evidence-based practice. It added that the review would look at how information about each baby’s condition was recorded and communicated among the clinical team and how decisions were made in the context of available resources. HIS has scheduled a series of stakeholder meetings with families, clinicians, and patient advocacy groups to discuss how the review will proceed, what information will be considered, and how findings will be communicated. A draft set of terms of reference is expected to be published in the coming weeks, with a final version to be issued after feedback from consultees. The families themselves have been offered the option of submitting their own accounts to the process. Some have indicated they will pursue independent channels to ensure their concerns are addressed even if the official review cannot consider their individual cases in full. Legal advisers for several families have warned that without broader scrutiny, families risk a sense that the system is protecting itself rather than protecting patients. The Clinical Negligence and Common Law bar associations have also weighed in, suggesting that while HIS may provide important recommendations for practice, they do not replace the need for independent public inquiry with statutory powers in cases involving child deaths. They note that a public inquiry would have powers to compel testimony, gather documents, and examine governance decisions at a scale that a programme of clinical review generally does not permit. NHS Ayrshire & Arran said it remained committed to patient safety and learning from adverse events. A spokesperson emphasised that the health board would cooperate with HIS and provide access to records and staff as required. “Our priority is to understand what happened and to implement improvements that prevent recurrence,” the spokesperson said. “We understand the anxiety of families and will keep them informed about the review’s progress and any findings that are publicly releasable.” But the operator of Crosshouse hospital has faced criticism in recent years for a perceived lack of transparency around other incidents in neonatal care. A number of families have argued that the hospital’s communications with relatives during highly stressful periods were inadequate and that important information was not always shared promptly. While hospital officials insist that every effort is made to keep families informed in a compassionate and timely manner, critics say this has not always been the case. Experts say the issue may reflect broader challenges in the national health service in Scotland, where neonatal units across several regional networks have faced pressures from rising birth rates and higher acuity among newborns. In some places, staffing challenges have been cited by unions as a factor that can jeopardize the safety and quality of care when there are high patient loads and limited senior cover at night. Proponents of a broader inquiry argue that such systemic issues should not be overlooked when examining individual tragic outcomes. The Scottish Government has acknowledged those concerns, stressing that the aim of the Crosshouse review is to generate concrete improvements that can be replicated across the country. It emphasised that the review is not intended to be punitive, but to identify gaps in care pathways and to strengthen governance and safety culture in neonatal units. But for families who have waited years for accountability and answers, yesterday’s developments offered little to ease the sense of frustration. One parent, who has spoken publicly in the past about their child’s death, said that the lack of a transparent, comprehensive process was “difficult to bear” and that the decision to exclude earlier cases could feed a perception that the health service is scanning for problems it can fix without confronting deeper questions about the way care is organised. Public health academic researchers have urged caution in interpreting the plan to limit the review’s scope. They say that while it is reasonable to focus on recent cases for which records are more robust, the absence of older cases could leave a blind spot in understanding how practice has evolved over time and whether earlier practices contributed to harm. They argue that learning from mistakes is often a function of tracing patterns over time and across different units within the same health system. In the meantime, patient safety activists have called for transparency around the review’s methods. They want to know how HIS will determine “preventability” and how it will weigh competing clinical judgments in cases where the outcome was fatal. They also want to understand what constitutes a “findable” improvement—whether the recommendations will be mandatory or advisory, and how health boards will be expected to demonstrate that changes have been implemented and sustained. The families have also raised questions about whether the review team will include external clinical experts with independence from the local health economy. They say that in the wake of high-profile failures in neonatal care elsewhere, external credibility can be crucial in restoring public confidence. HIS has indicated that it will consider applications from independent clinicians to join the review team, while also drawing on domestic experts in neonatal medicine, epidemiology, and patient safety. The cross-party response in Holyrood has reflected the tensions around how best to balance thoroughness with timeliness. Some MSPs have encouraged patience, stressing that the review’s conclusions could take months to finalise and that interim findings could be released along the way. Others have urged a more expansive scope, arguing that a narrow focus risks leaving families and clinicians with unanswered questions and missed opportunities for systemic improvement. Outside Westminster and Holyrood, families in other parts of the country have watched the Crosshouse case closely. A number of families who have faced similar losses have written to representatives asking for assurances that their own experiences will be considered in any national learning exercise. The Scottish government has said it is reviewing whether existing safeguards and national guidelines adequately support neonatal units during periods of high demand, and whether more needs to be done to ensure early recognition of deterioration and timely escalation of concerns. As the review proceeds, families and clinicians alike will be looking for a clear timetable and a transparent account of what is and is not included. A final report, with recommendations for national and local action, is expected to be published later next year. In the meantime, the families affected by Crosshouse continue to seek clarity about what happened to their babies, and why this new process has not encompassed every case that was promised to them. The broader question that arises from the current controversy is how best to translate lessons learned from tragic outcomes into real-world improvements that reach every neonatal unit across Scotland. The health service must show not only that it can identify failures, but that it can enact lasting changes that will protect newborns in all settings. And for the families whose babies never returned home, the need for answers remains urgent and enduring.

title: Biriyani is the quintessential celebratory dish in India and an aromatic delicacy that dazzles as a sublime one-dish meal, writes historian and food expert Pushpesh Pant.
text_ai: The 400-year-old city of Hyderabad is linked in popular mind for its signature biriyani as much as it is with the exquisitely constructed Charminar monument. The biriyani may have become a local landmark, but that doesn't stop people from asking, "Where did it come to India from and when?" Scholars caution that there may never be a single birthplace for biriyani. What is clearer is that in the Deccan, a dish of rice, meat and perfume-like spices was refined into something recognisable as a Hyderabadi biriyani, and then exported in kitchens and households across the subcontinent. The 17th and 18th centuries were pivotal: the Qutb Shahi sultans, and later the Nizams who ruled Hyderabad, cultivated a courtly cuisine that absorbed travellers and traders from Persia, Central Asia and the Gulf, and blended them with local stock and spice blends. Cooks experimented with proportions, with marination times, with the timing of frying onions and layering rice, with the drift of saffron and kewra, until a dish that could be served as a ceremonial centrepiece emerged. The word biriyani itself has been traced to Persian and Turkish linguistic families, though many in India prefer to describe biriyani as a culinary process rather than a fixed recipe. Common to almost all regional variants is a meticulous layering of partially cooked long-grain rice with marinated meat, enveloped in a steam-filled, sealed container so that the flavours mingle rather than burst apart. In Hyderabad, as in Lucknow and elsewhere, cooks adopted the dum pukht method—slow, gentle cooking in a sealed pot—to coax the meat to tenderness without losing its essence to heat. Hyderabadi biriyani is usually spoken of in two broad forms: kacchi, where raw meat is marinated and placed between layers of partially cooked rice, and then slow-cooked; and pakki, where the meat is pre-cooked and then folded through with rice. Each has its champions and its ritual admirers. What unites them is a fragrance that seems almost musical—the scent of fried onions, mint, coriander, saffron, and a light kiss of kewra or rose water. The result is a dish that looks simple, yet carries a history of kitchens where royal hospitality was a performance, and food a language used to mark alliances and celebrations. In the popular imagination, Hyderabad biriyani sits as a symbol of the city’s cosmopolitan past. Its success has helped to propel street-food stalls into institutions and, more recently, to attract global attention. Diners in the city and visitors from outside have played a part in shaping what counts as “authentic” Hyderabadi biriyani, even as purists argue for the fidelity of older recipes. What persists is a ritual of tasting—first a perfumed waft of spice, then the fork’s light lift of rice and meat, followed by the slow gratitude of shared plates among families and friends. Across the subcontinent, biriyani has travelled with the migrations of people, artisans and merchants. In Calcutta, Bombay, Chennai and beyond, regional differences grew as cooks adapted biriyani to local tastes and ingredients. In the south, for instance, biriyani styles often mingle with coconut, curry leaves, and hotter chilies; in the north, the impact of Mughal kitchens left a more saffron-tinted, jewel-like palate. In Pakistan, Sindhi biriyani shares the love of layered rice with a tangy, tomato-based tang, and in the Gulf, biriyani became a bridge between Indian culinary brilliance and Middle Eastern hospitality. And yet the dish continues to be a site of modern contest. Restaurateurs in Hyderabad and elsewhere regularly argue over what constitutes the “true” Hyderabadi biriyani, while home cooks in streets and homes alike defend family secrets as if they were heritage manuscripts. In an era of mass production, the challenge is preserving the slow-cooked tenderness and aromatic depth that many believe define the dish. If Pushpesh Pant is right, biriyani will always be more than a one-origin dish: it is a living archive of migration, trade, ritual and festivity. A plate of biriyani, after all, is a diary of journeys—the spice routes that braided together continents, and the shared table that keeps people talking, tasting and returning for another share. The next bite may bring a new argument about origin, but it will also continue to bind together a city, a country, and a family around a single, exquisitely scented, constantly reinvented dish.

title: Ulster moved to the top of the Pro12 table as a late Paddy Jackson penalty secured victory over the Dragons.
text_ai: Jackson's 78th-minute kick put Ulster ahead for the first time in the game. An Adam Hughes try helped the lively Dragons lead 10-0 before Sean Reidy's score cut the margin to 10-7 by half-time at Kingspan Stadium. Ulster had to weather a late rally from the Dragons, who threw everything at them in the closing minutes as they searched for a leveller that would have kept their hopes of an away win intact. But the defence held firm, with Ulster repelling a succession of quick-phase ball and contesting every breakdown to deny the visitors a meaningful sight of goal. The home side had started the second period with renewed bite, driving the Dragons back with a series of powerful carries from close to the 22 and a string of precision darts at the ruck. It looked as though Ulster might snipe their way into a lead during a tense spell, but the Dragons’ tackling and cover defence kept the scoreboard stubbornly still at 10-7 as the period wore on. Ulster’s fightback was grounded in pressure rather than spectacular breaks. They pinned Dragons deep in their own half for long spells, nudging and probing, and when the Dragons did get out, Ulster’s back three were swift to mop up the returns. The clean line-speed in defence prevented easy momentum for Dragons’ sharp runners, and the home team grew more confident with every successful hit in the contact area. There were glimpses of Ulster’s intent to press again in behind the visitors’ line, and the mood inside the ground suggested this one could tilt at any moment. title: For most of her life, Jessie Stocks has been surrounded by four grey walls and machines in Sheffield Children's Hospital.

title: Boris Johnson's office has warned senior officials at London's City Hall not to speak out in favour of staying in the European Union.

title: For the past 16 years, the electoral map for US presidential elections has been variations on a familiar theme.
text_ai: Ohio and Florida are the key battlegrounds. A handful of other states - including New Hampshire, Virginia, Colorado and Iowa - count as smaller prizes in the quest to the reach the magic number of 270 electoral votes. Across the last decade and a half, the two states alone have repeatedly determined who reaches the 270 mark and who falls outside it, forcing candidates to deliver their best case in person, in the airwaves and on the ground in a handful of counties rather than roam the country at large. Ohio and Florida have been far more than line items on a list of swing states. They function as litmus tests for the economy, for the mood of white working-class voters, for the fate of suburban voters whose loyalties have swung across both parties depending on the issue du jour. They are the places where a few thousand ballots in a handful of counties can tip a national outcome, and where campaigns spend more time and more money than in any other part of the country. To understand why those states hold such sway, it is necessary to look at the political and demographic shifts that have taken place since the 2008 election, when President Barack Obama first carried Ohio and Florida but failed to clinch the presidency in those same counties the way he had in other battlegrounds. Since then, the electoral map has been a mosaic that often refuses to change color at scale, even as the national mood shifts. A handful of states—New Hampshire, Virginia, Colorado and Iowa among them—have continued to offer prizes that can be decisive, albeit smaller in total than Ohio or Florida, and their margins have grown thinner as their own politics have become more complicated. In Ohio, the story is one of a state that has become more bifurcated along urban-rural lines. The cities—Cincinnati, Columbus, Cleveland—pull with a different gravitational force than the rural heartland and exurban belts that ring the state. The economy, once dominated by manufacturing, has diversified to service sectors and logistics, a change that has fed polarized views about trade, immigration and the role of government in the daily life of working families. Politically, the 2010s consolidated a pattern in which suburban voters—particularly those with college degrees—drifted toward the Democrats in some cycles, only to move back toward the Republicans when inflation and concerns about crime or national security rose to the top of the agenda. In 2020 and 2024, candidates understood that any effort to win the state would require a careful balance: addressing belt-tightening concerns at the kitchen-table level while not alienating the more conservative wings that have long defined the state’s political backbone. Florida remains a more mercurial proposition. It is a blend of national conscience and local volatility: a large immigrant population, a robust retiree sector, and a sprawling suburban periphery that can swing from one election to the next. The state’s Cuban-American communities have played a unique role in shaping votes on issues such as foreign policy and sanctions, while younger Latino voters in coastal counties have shown a more mixed pattern, sometimes aligning with the Republicans on economic issues and with Democrats on issues like the environment and education. Then there is the perennial drama of Florida’s media market, where surrogates, donors and political action committees converge to test messages across a spectrum of audiences inside a single county and across the state’s famous weather patterns, which can seem as volatile as the polling numbers. The map’s rest-of-country players—New Hampshire, Virginia, Colorado, Iowa—have become laboratories for shifts that could leave the core battleground states feeling less decisive than in the past. New Hampshire’s appeal has long rested on a compact, intensive retail-politics culture. It rewards candidates who excel in town halls and one-on-one conversation, demanding a granular approach to the questions that matters most to voters in small communities. Virginia’s political geography tells a different story: a state that has trended blue in presidential years but contains red pockets in rural areas that can still dent margins in statewide races. Colorado has been a laboratory for demographic change and the increasing political weight of educated suburban voters, even as rural areas in the west persist as conservative counterweights. Iowa, once seen as the forecasting ground for presidential fortunes, has become a test case for how far a candidate can appeal to white working-class voters without alienating the broader coalition the party needs. All this means that the 270-vote target remains a moving object, shifting with every census, every demographic trend, every change in turnout. The 2020 election underscored a simple truth: even as a national mood can flip, the map can behave differently from year to year, depending on the issues that define the moment and the way voters perceive the economy and public safety. In recent cycles, the surge of early and mail voting, the proliferation of targeted digital messaging, and the role of grassroots organising in key counties have reshaped how candidates allocate time and resources. Campaign trail strategy now begins far earlier than it did a generation ago. The earliest phases are usually less about broadly persuasive arguments and more about carving a coalition that can survive the inevitable twists of a campaign—local concerns translated into national policy positions, community-level concerns turned into macro questions about inflation, healthcare costs and the national debt. In practice, this means dozens of ads, dozens of town-hall visits, and the kind of data-driven microtargeting that tracks which households have responded to which messages, and which neighborhoods are likely to see the highest turnout on election day. Analysts warn that the map’s stability should not be mistaken for predictability. The same states that appear to be anchors can shift given a handful of issues that tilt voter priorities in a particular direction. The economy continues to be the most influential determinant of voting behavior. When inflation is high or the job market feels unsettled, voters in both parties tend to demand more aggressive economic solutions, and incumbents often pay a steep price when those promises fail to translate into tangible relief. Conversely, in periods of strong growth, a candidate’s record on jobs and wages can trump concerns over social issues, allowing the incumbent to pad margins in traditionally red or blue states and shrink the margins in swing states that define the national outcome. The role of demographics cannot be overemphasized. The suburbs, especially in and around cities like Columbus, Tampa, and the denser corridors of Denver and Phoenix, have become the critical swing laboratories. Voters without a college degree in these areas have repeatedly proved pivotal, sometimes supporting a Republican ticket when the economic message resonated, sometimes turning toward Democrats when social issues and healthcare policy dominated the news cycle. In Florida, the fast-growing Hispanic and immigrant communities have become more important in deciding statewide races, particularly when candidates articulate credible plans for the economy and, separately, for issues such as education and crime. In Ohio, the coalition of white working-class voters with more affluent suburban households has been the fulcrum of many campaigns, a dynamic that has forced both major parties to work to avoid alienating any single subgroup. The 2024 cycle demonstrated that winning the map is as much about turnout and logistics as it is about the rhetoric of policy. The ground game—how campaigns organise volunteers, mobilise voters, and secure early votes—has become a differentiator between campaigns that perform well on television and those that actually convert airtime into ballots. Early voting has altered the tempo of campaigns: more time is spent on persuasion before the election, while a larger share of votes is cast before November, reducing the impact of famous final-week events. The campaigns that managed to sustain enthusiasm from summer through October tended to close the gap in key states more effectively, and the difference in margins often came down to which campaign could translate a few extra points of turnout into actual votes in a few critical counties. Redistricting after the 2020 census introduced another layer of complexity. Several states redrew lines in ways that altered the balance between urban cores and rural peripheries, and moved some communities into districts where the partisan tilt is less predictable. Courts played a role in a handful of disputes, ruling on the extent to which maps could reflect political affiliation without suppressing the voting power of particular communities. The long-term consequence of these changes could be more stability in some regions and greater volatility in others, depending on how population shifts unfold in the coming decade. For now, the effect is a map that remains recognisable in its most consequential regard—two regional anchors that determine the pace and outcome of the race—but with nuanced changes in the surrounding counties that can make all the difference on election day. Voting rights and access remain a persistent subtext of the national conversation. In an era of heightened scrutiny, states have pursued a mix of policies intended to safeguard the integrity of the vote while addressing concerns about convenience and access. Jurisdictions have experimented with same-day registration, extended early-voting windows, and adjustments to absentee-ballot rules. The balance struck in each state shapes not only turnout but the perception of the election’s legitimacy—a factor that, in turn, influences how voters feel about the competitiveness of the race and whether they believe every vote has an equal chance of counting. The national narrative of the race will also be shaped by issues that are not strictly political in the narrow sense. Climate resilience, energy policy, healthcare costs, and the direction of the economy all resonate differently across geographic lines. In Florida, for example, energy policy and the hurricane season’s impact on insurance markets become acute concerns for voters who feel their daily lives directly affected by national decisions. In Ohio, the same voters may be more focused on manufacturing jobs, wage trends, and the practicalities of small-business survival in a region that has faced structural economic shifts for years. In both places, candidates must demonstrate not just policy acumen but credibility on the issues that matter most to households trying to make ends meet. The role of third-party candidates, long a feature of American elections, has settled into a pattern of affecting margins rather than deciding elections outright in most cycles. In recent years, a portion of the electorate has shown willingness to consider non-main party options for reasons ranging from policy dissatisfaction to disillusionment with the two major parties’ ability to deliver tangible results. Campaigns have learned to address this space without letting it crowd the central argument, nudging voters toward their preferred path while avoiding a perception that a protest vote could undermine a candidate’s chances. As the calendar moves toward the next election, analysts expect the map to retain its familiar core with Ohio and Florida continuing to set the tone for national strategy while Virginia, Colorado, New Hampshire and Iowa provide the weather-vane signals that pollsters and operatives watch most closely. The practical reality, however, is that campaigns will be forced to contend with a dynamic landscape that can shift even in the last weeks before voters go to the polls. A few unexpected events—economic shocks, national security concerns, or a major policy breakthrough—could tilt the balance in a way that reshapes expectations long before Election Day. What does this mean for the public, the voters whose ballots will decide the next presidency? It means unsurprisingly that engagement matters more than ever. Voters who stay informed, who understand the policy implications of the candidates’ plans, and who participate in the process at every stage—through registration, early voting, and on Election Day—will have a meaningful influence on the outcome. title: When Jose Mourinho walked out of his BBC interview after Wednesday's 0-0 draw with Hull, it was the latest example of a Premier League manager taking exception to a reporter's questions.
text_ai: So what is it like to be the person behind the microphone when an interview goes wrong? We asked reporters from Match of the Day, BBC Radio 5 live and BBC Scotland to share their most excruciating experiences. The recurring theme is not simply frustration at a question, but the fragile line between scrutiny and dialogue in a sport built on sound bites and spin. In a landscape where managers are treated as public figures, questions are part of the job. Yet as one veteran broadcaster recalls, the most uncomfortable moments arise not from what is asked, but from what a manager believes has already been decided about him, his team, or his club before the interview begins. Open and honest interrogation is prized in BBC sports journalism. But there is a countercurrent: high-stakes, high-visibility football means tempers flare when a manager feels a line of inquiry is unfair, repetitive, or designed to trap him. The result can be a tense room, a clipped response, or a sudden walkout that becomes a talking point far beyond the ground. For a reporter, the aim is to illuminate performance with context—tactics, squad rotation, injuries, and the broader narrative of a season. In practice, that can clash with post-match adrenaline. A manager who has just endured ninety minutes of intense pressure may feel he has just endured a personal onslaught. The reporter, meanwhile, is attempting to translate the on-pitch drama into a story that resonates with fans who did not see the match. One of the enduring memories among correspondents is the moment a question lands in the silence after the final whistle. The pitch invites near silence, the stadium lights cast long shadows, and a microphone becomes a conduit to an emotional verdict. It is here that perception of fairness becomes a moral measure of a broadcaster’s credibility. Reporters speak of balancing candour with restraint—pressing for clarity on decisions that shaped the result while avoiding prodding into private territory or rehearsed talking points. The danger, several reporters say, lies in a question that treads too close to a manager’s self-image: a critique veiled as inquiry, or an assertion presented as fact. In those moments, a post-match interview can feel less like journalism and more like a confrontation. The best interviewers navigate with phrasing that invites reflection rather than confrontation, coupling tough questions with a tone that signals respect for the manager’s expertise and time. But not every controversial moment follows a single recipe. Some managers respond to questions about tactics with a concise defence of their method, while others use the forum to air broader grievances about media coverage, refereeing decisions, or the pressures of modern football. The result can be a wide-ranging rebuttal that reveals as much about the manager’s temperament as the match itself. The press room, too, shapes the experience. The room can feel intimate or intimidating, depending on the presence of players, coaching staff, and security. The overhead cameras, the constant hum of the newsroom, and the clock’s inexorable countdown all contribute to a sense of urgency. In that environment, a reporter’s style—whether brisk and direct or careful and exploratory—has a direct bearing on the mood of the exchange. Several of the most memorable episodes crystallise around a single line or moment that seems to capture a wider dynamic. A manager’s decision to stand by a squad or a tactical plan after a draw can translate into a refusal to acknowledge fault or a demand for time to reflect. When a journalist presses on why a substitution did not yield the expected result, the response can pivot from explanation to exasperation, and from there to exit. The ethics of post-match interviews are debated among editors and unions. Dozens of questions have been debated in newsroom staff rooms about how to handle a manager who has begun to repeat a line in the same forum, or who appears to be isolating himself from the wider media scrum by returning to a vehicle before the final questions have been asked. Some editors advocate a firm line: if a manager refuses, the session ends; others argue for giving space, allowing a manager to decompress, and returning to questions with renewed openness. However the most telling approach is to plan. A well-briefed reporter will study the manager’s previous posts, the club’s recent form, and potential flashpoints in the season’s arc. With that preparation comes a sense of proportion about what is valuable to fans: how injuries influenced selection, whether the system is sustainable, and whether the club’s approach to youth development is paying dividends. Preparation also includes understanding the human element: fatigue, personal fatigue, or a sense of being misrepresented in the media. Beyond the individual interviews there is a broader conversation about the role of the media in football. Critics argue the press magnifies missteps and encourages sensationalism, while defenders say scrutiny is essential for accountability and for fans to understand the reasoning behind decisions that affect teams and communities. In practice the balance is difficult to strike. The sport’s owners and executives courts attention as a matter of business, while journalists chase clarity and truth under the glare of social media and a 24-hour news cycle. In parallel, there is a growing awareness among managers that the post-match moment has changed. Critics point to social media as amplifying any misstep, instantly broadcasting it to millions and shaping public perception before a full transcript can be produced. Some managers have responded by accelerating media duties to contain a narrative, or by using the room to articulate longer-term strategies, thereby reframing the immediate result within a bigger picture. Among the most challenging episodes cited by reporters are those in which a manager appears to misconstrue the premise of the question, or interprets it through a lens of personal grievance. In those cases, the interview can devolve into a defensive loop: question, justification, reassertion, and eventually, exit. The best antidote, according to several veterans, is to persevere with a calm, balanced approach, asking follow-ups that avoid piling into a single line of thinking and instead map the broader reasoning behind decisions. There is also value in good timing. Some managers are more receptive immediately after a game than in the days that follow when disappointment or triumph can crystallise into longer-form media engagements. The timing of questions—whether during the post-match ritual, a midweek press conference, or a pre-match media briefing—affects not only the level of candour but also the potential for misinterpretation. A well-timed question can yield a thoughtful, constructive response; a poorly timed one can provoke a defensive reaction. Analysts and editors stress the importance of accuracy. A single misquote or misinterpretation can escalate tensions and distort the record. In the heat of the moment, even a minor factual error can become a target for rebuttal, so fact-checking and precise recall of events are crucial. This is particularly true in an era when teams field a large squad, with several injuries, suspensions, and tactical adjustments that can matter as much as the result itself. Looking ahead, there are shifts in how post-match duties are conceived. Some clubs have introduced structured media briefings that include a clear outline of what will be discussed, with time allotted for questions on specific topics. Others are experimenting with mixed formats, combining on-pitch analysis with written transcripts or video debriefs to give fans a fuller picture of the match’s complexities. The objective is not to placate critics but to foster a more informed, respectful exchange that serves the interests of the sport. Of course, there is a human cost to these exchanges. Reporters, who often work long hours under tight deadlines, carry the emotional weight of what they hear. A manager’s frustration can reverberate through a newsroom, affecting colleagues who must craft a measured, accurate account under pressure. The same is true for club staff and players who may be present in the room; a tense moment can cast a shadow over a team’s morale in the hours that follow. In the end, the public consciousness of football hinges on these conversations. Scores and results capture attention; but the conversations that follow shape the narrative of a club, a season, and sometimes a career. The reporter’s task is to translate the intensity of the moment into questions that illuminate decisions, explain strategy, and hold power to account—without amplifying a moment that could compromise the trust between the press and the teams they cover. For fans, these moments are part of the theatre of football. They can be frustrating, revealing, or simply human. They remind us that behind every match is a network of decisions, pressures, and goals that extend far beyond the final whistle. And they remind journalists of their responsibility: to pursue truth with fairness, to challenge with context, and to report what matters with clarity and restraint. As the season unfolds, the relationship between managers and reporters will continue to evolve. Some managers will welcome the chance to articulate their vision in the post-match arena; others will prefer to retreat to the dressing room or the sanctity of quiet reflection. The BBC’s role remains to bring readers and viewers closer to the realities of the game, through clear reporting, accountable questioning, and a commitment to accuracy, regardless of which manager dominates the headlines. For those who help tell the story—from the senior editors to the youngest trainees—the lessons are enduring: preparation matters, tone matters, and time matters. The post-match interview is not just about the scoreline; it is about how a club interprets its own performance, how a journalist interprets the performance for the audience, and how the sport, in its most visible moments, negotiates scrutiny with dignity. In the weeks ahead, you will hear more voices sharing their experiences, both the thorny and the instructive. The aim is not to sensationalise, but to understand the dynamics at work in a sport where 90 minutes can determine a season, and where the microphone is both a gift and a gauntlet, depending on how it is used. As for Jose Mourinho’s moment of exit, it stands as a cautionary tale and a talking point—one incident in a long career where the boundary between inquiry and provocation is carefully policed, and where the craft of interviewing remains a discipline in its own right. The BBC will continue to approach these moments with rigor, fairness, and a commitment to the truth, always mindful that the ultimate objective is a clearer, more complete understanding of the game for every listener and viewer.
